South Carolina Cannabis & Hemp Research — AUDITED, Parts 0–12

Last audited: 24 October 2026

Scope. This single self-contained file merges two independent primary-source audits into one Parts 0–12 dossier: Part 1A / Part 2A audit Run 1 (Parts 0–6: headlines, laws, taxes, local rules, licence types, licence data sources, market data), and Part 1B / Part 2B audit Run 2 (Parts 7–12: hemp licences, properties, regulators/history, tribal/interstate, operations, consumer/social), carried from the previously delivered Run 2 audited file. No section was dropped from either run. Where the Run 1 audit resolves a flag that the Run 2 audit left open, the resolution is stated in a merge note — Run 2 verdicts were not silently changed. This file supersedes the Run 2-only audited file for combined use; the Run 2-only file itself was not modified.

How to read it. Part 1 is the audit record: Section | Claim | Verdict | Primary source (URL) | Corrected wording, followed by everything still unverified and where to confirm it. Part 2 is the corrected rewrite: every section and detail from the originals is retained; only what the audit changed was changed, in place, everywhere it appears. Proposed licence types and taxes are labelled PROPOSED with bill number and status — never presented as law. [VERIFY] / [UNAVAILABLE] flags remain only on items still unresolved. Every fact keeps a source link next to it where the original provided one or the audit supplied one.

Personal-contact rule. No individual licence holder's personal phone number or email is reproduced anywhere in this file. Agency public contacts only. SCDA pilot counts are given without individual names.

Federal baseline (given, not re-audited)

  • Scheduling is split — 91 FR 22714, effective 28 April 2026: FDA-approved cannabis products and state-licensed medical marijuana are Schedule III. All other marijuana, including all adult-use, remains Schedule I. The broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is NOT final.
  • IRS 280E: Treasury has said rescheduling generally removes 280E as a bar for businesses no longer dealing in Schedule I/II substances (guidance forthcoming). Adult-use remains fully subject to 280E.
  • Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes legal effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026 to only the provisions excluding cannabinoids not naturally produced or synthesised. The full total-THC definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply after 11 December 2026.
  • USDA: enforcement of the DEA-registered-laboratory hemp testing requirement is delayed until 31 December 2026.
  • Federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider in force through 11 December 2026.
  • No federal cannabis banking law enacted.
  • South Carolina: SC has no state-licensed medical programme, so marijuana remains Schedule I in South Carolina. Julian's Law is NOT a state-licensed medical programme; FDA-approved cannabis products are a separate federal Schedule III category and must not be described as Schedule I.

Audit rules applied in both runs. Primary sources only: SC Code of Laws and bill pages on scstatehouse.gov, SC Code of Regulations and State Register, SC Department of Agriculture, SC Department of Revenue, SLED, SC Department of Public Health, SC Department of Environmental Services, AG official opinions, SC Election Commission, and official county/city/town sites and codes. News, law-firm blogs, trade press, directories and AI summaries never confirm a fact — they leave it Unverified. Every claim gets one verdict: Confirmed, Corrected, Removed, or Unverified (with Partially confirmed / Split where a cluster used it). Conflicting figures were resolved to the most authoritative official source, with the reason stated. Every pending bill's status was checked on scstatehouse.gov accounting for the two-year session cycle. The blocked S.53 bill page (sess126_2025-2026/bills/53.htm, 429 in a prior session) was NOT re-opened; S.53 was verified via its billsearch page and bill-text search results.

(b) 12 factors confirmed (statements of owner/person in control; proximity to controlled substances; residue; direct/circumstantial evidence of intent to deliver to persons the owner knows/should reasonably know intend unlawful use; instructions; descriptive materials; national/local advertising; manner displayed for sale; whether owner is a legitimate supplier of like items such as a licensed tobacco distributor/dealer; ratio of object sales to total business sales; existence/scope of legitimate community uses; expert testimony). History: 1982 Act No. 400, §2. The rule's application is corrected in the next row: it does not make every 126th-session bill "dead" as of the report's access date.

§2.1Rate 6% state: §12-36-910(A) imposes sales tax on gross proceeds of retail sales of tangible personal property (§12-36-910 is a 5% base; §12-36-1110 adds 1%, for an effective 6%); §12-36-1310(A) imposes a complementary 6% use taxCorrected (use-tax pinpoint)https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t12c036.php (§12-36-910: "A sales tax, equal to five percent of the gross proceeds of sales, is imposed upon every person engaged or continuing within this State in the business of selling tangible personal property at retail" ; §12-36-1110: "an additional sales, use, and casual excise tax equal to one percent" ; §12-36-1310(A): use tax "at the rate of five percent of the sales price of the property")Keep the 6% state figure, but correct the pinpoint language: §12-36-910(A) imposes 5%, §12-36-1110 adds 1% = 6% state sales tax; §12-36-1310(A) imposes 5% use tax, with the additional 1% under §12-36-1110 giving a combined 6% use-tax figure. Do NOT write "§12-36-1310(A) imposes a complementary 6% use tax" — (A) itself says five percent. Also note the §12-36-1110 exceptions: the additional 1% does not apply to amounts taxed under §12-36-920(A) (accommodations), nor to items subject to a maximum tax under §12-36-2110, nor to "the sale of unprepared food which may be lawfully purchased with United States Department of Agriculture food coupons" — see the unprepared-food correction below.

§3.3 ConwayConway was still drafting in Dec 2025: Conway Planning Commission, 12 Dec 2025 (secondary summary): staff outlined options including confining such uses to light/heavy industrial districts, conditional use, or BZA special exception, citing Myrtle Beach's overlay as an example and sample spacing of 2,640 ft (½ mile) from another smoke/vape shop and 1,500 ft from schools, childcare, parks and youth facilities; asked to draft ordinance language; no adoption reported — proposal, not lawCorrected (SUPERSEDED — adopted 4 May 2026)https://www.conwaysc.gov/Current UDO (5.4.26).pdf?t=20260606122900437 (City of Conway UDO, adopted 12 Dec 2011, last amended 4 May 2026, §5.1.37 [ZA2026-05-04 (O)]) — see full corrected wording below. Secondary meeting history: https://citizenportal.ai/articles/7217049/South-Carolina/Horry-County/Conway/Conway-planning-staff-outlines-options-to-restrict-vape-shops-and-payday-lenders-commission-asks-for-draft-ordinance (AI-generated summary — secondary only; do not cite it for the law).MAJOR CORRECTION — replace the "still drafting" paragraph with adopted law: "ADOPTED: Conway UDO §5.1.37, Tobacco, Vape, and Smoke Shop Establishments [ZA2026-05-04 (O)] (UDO last amended 4 May 2026). Definition: a retail establishment whose primary or principal business is the sale of tobacco products, vaping products, CANNABIS-DERIVED CONSUMABLES, smoking devices, or related paraphernalia. Permitted in the CC, NC, MU, HC, LI and HI Zoning Districts, provided: (A.1) no location within one-half mile (2,640 feet) of another Tobacco, Vape, or Smoke Shop establishment, regardless of whether it is within City limits or unincorporated Horry County, and regardless of same parcel/building/multi-tenant development; (A.2) no location within 1,500 feet of: (a) K-12 educational facilities, public or private; (b) childcare facilities; (c) youth/teen centers or clubs; (d) religious institutions; (e) Community Support Facilities; (f) Outpatient Treatment Facilities; (g) public parks, playgrounds, and publicly owned recreational facilities, including designated multi-use trails; (h) public libraries; (i) other public facilities primarily serving children, youth, or vulnerable populations; (A.3) residential proximity: administrative approval by the Zoning Administrator where the establishment does NOT share a property line with a residential use or property zoned for residential development, but BZA SPECIAL EXCEPTION approval where it DOES share a common property line with a parcel containing a residential use or zoned for residential development (within City limits or unincorporated Horry County); (A.4) measurement: straight line from the closest property line of the proposed establishment's parcel to the closest property line of the protected parcel, without regard to intervening structures, rights-of-way, or ownership; (B) hours: no operation between 9:00 p.m. and 8:00 a.m.; (C) signage: clear signage stating applicable age-restriction requirements under state and federal law, conspicuously at each public entrance; (D) nonconformities: a legally operating, properly licensed establishment not in compliance at adoption is deemed nonconforming under Art. 12; (E) licensing: maintain all applicable state and federal licences; failure to comply may result in suspension or revocation of zoning approval AND business licensing. The Dec 2025 proposal figures (2,640 ft / 1,500 ft) match the adopted text exactly — the proposal became law. The Dec 2025 meeting account is retained ONLY as history (secondary, AI-generated summary — cite with that flag, never as the law)." At merge time, confirm no Conway amendment after 4 May 2026.

§3.3 Myrtle BeachOBEOD ban — §1807: within the OBEOD, prohibited retail uses include (1) smoke shops and tobacco stores; (2) merchandising of tobacco paraphernalia or products containing CBD (lotions, oils, food); (3) tobacco merchandising beyond incidental (>10% of inventory); (4) sexually oriented material; declared immediately nonconforming on passage 14 Aug 2018, amortization to 31 Dec 2018, business-licence suspension/revocation for continued violationConfirmed (details upgraded from Run 2-flagged, with host caveat)https://law.justia.com/cases/south-carolina/supreme-court/2023/28151.html (Ani Creation, Inc. v. City of Myrtle Beach (2023), court's recitation of §1807.D–F); official city zoning code text for §1807.A (purpose/intent) retrieved in prior sessionUpgrade the Run 2-flagged details to Confirmed on the court's own recitation, with this caveat stated in the merged file: the opinion text was retrieved via Justia's reproduction, not the court's own PDF. Confirmed recitation: §1807.D prohibited retail uses are (1) smoke shops and tobacco stores; (2) any merchandising of tobacco paraphernalia or products containing CBD, such as lotions, oils, and food; (3) any merchandising of tobacco products more than incidental (i.e. more than 10% of the store's inventory); (4) any merchandising of sexually oriented material. Prohibited uses declared immediately nonconforming upon passage on 14 Aug 2018 (§1807.E); affected businesses given until 31 Dec 2018 to cease the nonconforming part of their retail offerings; continued prohibited use subjects a business to suspension or revocation of its business licence (§1807.F). Suit filed 19 Dec 2018, shortly before the amortization period ended. Note: §1807 code definitions (e.g. CANNABIS PRODUCT excluding marijuana as defined by §44-53-110(27)(a); CANNABIS DISPENSING BUSINESS as a business offering CBD/cannabis/derivative products) are CODE definitions, not state-law definitions — do not quote them as state law.

§3.3 West ColumbiaZoning Ordinance §705.1.37 (C-2 General Commercial): "Hookah lounge, vape lounge, smoke shop, vape shop, and CBD oil shop permitted as a conditional use," subject to: "The lot line of any property whereupon exists a [listed shop] shall not be located within a one-thousand-foot radius of the lot line of any lot zoned for or used as residential use."Corrected (wrong pinpoint; incomplete conditions; wrong use list)https://westcolumbiasc.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Zoning-Ordinance-2004-Official-May-2025-web-copy_July-2026.pdf (May 2025 official copy, July 2026 PDF)Correct to: "In the May 2025 official code, §705.1.37 is SEXUALLY ORIENTED BUSINESSES per §809 — NOT the smoke-shop provision. The smoke-shop conditional use sits as unnumbered subsection A. under the Retail use in each district: C-2 General Commercial §705.1.5.A; LM Light Manufacturing §707.1.6.A; HM (heavy manufacturing) §708.1.6.A — identical conditions in all three. Use list in those provisions: 'Tobacco Store, Smoke Shop, Vape Shop (NAICS 453991), and Hookah Lounge, Vape Lounge (NAICS 713990)'. 'CBD oil shop' does NOT appear in those conditional-use lists; it appears ONLY in the Redevelopment District prohibition (§711.5.C(i) — see below). Whether a CBD-only shop falls under 'smoke shop'/'vape shop' is a Zoning Administrator interpretation — flag it, do not decide it. Conditions (all three districts, 8 total): (1) lot line not within a one-thousand-foot radius of the lot line of any lot zoned for or used as residential use; (2) lot line not within a one-thousand-foot radius of the lot line of another such LEGAL tobacco store, smoke shop, vape shop, hookah lounge, or vape lounge; (3) lot line not within a one-thousand-foot radius of any public or private K-12 school, library, church or other place of religious worship, youth center, day care center, park, playground or playing field; (4) on-site consumption of alcoholic beverages prohibited; (5) establishment must comply with applicable state and federal laws; (6) signs shall not include words or images referencing illicit substances (any Schedule 1 drug, substance, or chemical under the Controlled Substances Act); (7) use of LED accent lights prohibited; (8) closed between 7:00 PM and 9:00 AM. The report's single residential-buffer condition is therefore incomplete — the shop-to-shop buffer, the sensitive-use buffer, hours, signage and LED conditions were omitted."

Baseline box (p. 1, before Part 0)"state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); all adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I; IRS 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity and remains fully applicable to adult-use; PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026 but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026, after which the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply; USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026; the federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026; there is no federal cannabis banking law."Matches baseline, with one qualifier omittedGiven federal baseline (not re-audited)Keep, adding the omitted Treasury qualifier: "IRS 280E: Treasury has said rescheduling generally removes 280E as a bar for businesses no longer dealing in Schedule I/II substances (guidance forthcoming)." The report's "generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity" is consistent with the baseline in substance but drops both the Treasury attribution and the "guidance forthcoming" qualifier — add both. All dates in the box (28 Apr 2026; 12 Nov 2026; 11 Dec 2026; 31 Dec 2026) match the baseline.
Central finding (p. 1, note box)"South Carolina has no state-licensed medical marijuana programme, no adult-use programme, and no state cannabis licence. The only current medical exception is the narrow Julian's Law low-THC/CBD carve-out. Therefore, under the split-scheduling baseline, marijuana remains Schedule I in South Carolina in practical effect: there is no SC state-licensed medical activity to which the Schedule III move can attach, and SC's own Schedule I list still includes marijuana and THC. Whether [DPH] will act under §44-53-160(C) to conform state schedules to the federal change is [VERIFY — no DPH Schedule III conforming update was located]."Matches baselineGiven federal baseline (not re-audited)Keep. "In practical effect" is accurate framing, not a contradiction: SC's own Schedule I list (§44-53-190(D), items 11 Marijuana and 18 THC, confirmed in Run 2) still lists marijuana/THC, and no SC state-licensed medical activity exists to attach Schedule III to. Add for completeness that FDA-approved cannabis products are a separate federal Schedule III category (stated in the baseline box, not repeated here) — do not describe FDA-approved products as Schedule I in SC. The DPH [VERIFY] flag stands (Run 2: no conforming entry located).

Part 1B below is carried unchanged from the Run 2 audited file (24 October 2026), except for these bracketed reconciliations from the Run 1 audit: (1) SCDOR Retail License $50 per location is now CONFIRMED on dor.sc.gov — delete any “secondary — Verify” flag for that fee in Part 1B/Part 2B. (2) Operation Ganjapreneur follow-up date is 26 March 2026 (DEA mirror of the AG release) and “Midlands” stands (December release opened directly in the Run 1 Part 0 audit). (3) §44-53-391 is confirmed on the current scstatehouse.gov Code page and §44-53-393 (fentanyl test strips) is added wherever paraphernalia is discussed. (4) §46-55-10(9) unprocessed/raw-material exclusion sentence is verified verbatim on the current Code page. (5) §44-53-450(C) “summary court” ($150) comprises magistrate + municipal courts — Run 2's $150 magistrate / $150 municipal listing is the same $150 courts, not a different fee. No other Run 2 verdict was changed by the Run 1 audit.

Scope of this audit. The file audited here was Run 2, Parts 7–12 only (Part 7 Hemp Licences, Part 8 Cannabis-Zoned Properties, Part 9 Regulators and History, Part 10 Tribal and Interstate, Part 11 Operations Rules, Part 12 Consumer and Social Rules, plus Combined Research Notes). Run 1, Parts 0–6, was not in the attachment and was not re-audited here; Run 1 is used only as a cross-reference. The corrected rewrite in Part 2 therefore covers Parts 7–12 plus the combined notes only. It does not pretend to be a corrected Parts 0–12 dossier.

Method. Primary sources only: SC Code of Laws and bill pages on scstatehouse.gov, SC Code of Regulations / State Register, SC Department of Agriculture, SC Department of Revenue, SLED, SC Department of Public Health, SC Department of Environmental Services, Attorney General official opinions, SC Election Commission, and official county/city/town sites and codes. Nothing was confirmed from news, law-firm blogs, trade press, or AI summaries; where only a secondary source exists the item is marked Unverified. Every claim below carries one verdict: Confirmed, Corrected, Removed, or Unverified. Conflicting figures were resolved to the most authoritative official source, with the reason stated. Links were checked; broken or wrong links were replaced with the correct official URL. For any licence holder listed as an individual, no personal phone number or email is reproduced — name plus a link to the official source only. (Agency public contacts are retained.)

Federal baseline (given — not re-audited; only checked that the report states it correctly). Scheduling is split. Final rule 91 FR 22714 (effective 28 April 2026): FDA-approved cannabis products and state-licensed medical marijuana are Schedule III. All other marijuana, including all adult-use, remains Schedule I. The broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is NOT final. IRS 280E: Treasury has said rescheduling generally removes 280E as a bar for businesses no longer dealing in Schedule I/II substances (guidance forthcoming); adult-use activity remains fully subject to 280E. Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes legal effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026 to only the provisions excluding cannabinoids not naturally produced or synthesised. The full total-THC definition and the 0.4 mg per container cap apply after 11 December 2026. USDA delayed enforcement of the DEA-registered-laboratory hemp testing requirement until 31 December 2026. The federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider is in force through 11 December 2026. No federal cannabis banking law has been enacted. South Carolina application: South Carolina has no state-licensed medical programme, so no SC marijuana qualifies for the federal Schedule III state-licensed-medical category; Julian's Law is not a state-licensed medical programme; marijuana remains Schedule I in South Carolina (FDA-approved cannabis products are a separate federal Schedule III category and must not be described as Schedule I). No statement in Parts 7–12 was found contradicting the baseline, but the report omitted the banking, 2024-proposal, and rider sentences; they are added in Part 2. The report's dating of the full PL 119-37 cap to 12 November 2026 was corrected to after 11 December 2026.

How to read the table. “Corrected wording” is the wording used in Part 2. Rows are grouped Part 7, Part 8, Part 10, Part 11, Part 12, federal/cross-cutting, and combined notes; Part 9 rows are inserted in Part 9 order when the Part 9 cluster table is available. Where a row says a figure is “RESOLVED”, the conflict is closed and the flag is removed from Part 2; where it says [VERIFY] or [UNAVAILABLE], the flag is deliberately retained in Part 2.

§12.4Headline (secondary consensus): NO marijuana-specific expungement process and NO automatic expungement for marijuana convictions; general relief narrow, primarily certain misdemeanors; except 30-day misdemeanors, the person must initiate the process; Route 1 — Conditional discharge §44-53-450 (no prior conviction under the article or any state/federal marijuana/stimulant/depressant/hallucinogenic statute; pleads/found guilty of possession under §44-53-370(c)–(d) or §44-53-375(A); court without entering judgment of guilt and with accused’s consent may defer proceedings, place on probation incl. treatment/rehabilitation if available; on violation court may enter adjudication of guilt; on fulfilment court shall discharge/dismiss — not a conviction, but a nonpublic SLED record retained for later prior-offence determinations; discharge/dismissal only once; on dismissal person may apply for expungement of all official records (other than nonpublic record) — §44-53-450(B); fee $350 general sessions, $150 summary, waivable/reducible only for indigency; last amendment shown 2010 Act No. 273, eff. 2 June 2010); Route 2 — First-offence magistrates-court conviction §22-5-910 (≤30 days or $500 fine, or both; after 3 years from conviction may apply to circuit court; exclusions: motor-vehicle operation, Title 50 / points/suspension/enhanced-penalty, Ch. 25 Title 16 except first-offence CDV under §16-25-20 (5 years); marijuana application: first-offence simple possession ≤1 oz (misdemeanor, ≤30 days or $100–$200) fits the 30-day category, hence “3 years from conviction” if conditional discharge/PTI not used); Route 3 — First-offence Title 44 Ch. 53 Art. 3 possession §22-5-930: “Bill text only” from 2017–2018 H.3209 Comm Sub — 3 years from conviction, no other convictions in period, no expungement if pending charges, no more than once, no expungement if conditional discharge within prior 5 years (marijuana) / 10 years (other drug), expungement even if conviction pre-dated effective date, SLED nonpublic record — “NOT confirmed current law. [VERIFY — open current §22-5-930 before quoting it as law.] Do NOT present H.3209 text as current law without that check”; Route 4 — Dismissal/nolle prosequi/not guilty §17-1-40; AG opinion 21 May 2013 (McCurdy) example: simple possession under §44-53-370(d)(4) [old numbering, now (d)(5)] may eventually be destroyed/expunged via conditional discharge (§44-53-450), PTI (§17-22-150), or 3 years after first-offense conviction (§22-5-910); Route 5 — PTI §17-22-150(a); Route 6 — Youthful Offender Act §22-5-920 (5 years after completion if no other convictions); Route 7 — Other authorisations §17-22-910 (formerly §17-22-310, 2007–2008 Bill 110 text): (1) §34-11-90(e), (2) §44-53-450(b) conditional discharge for simple possession of marijuana or hashish, (3) §22-5-910, (4) §22-5-920, (5) §56-5-750(f), (6) §17-22-150(a), (7) §17-1-40 except §17-22-950, (8) §20-7-8525 (now recodified — check current juvenile citation), (9) §17-22-530(a), (10) any other authorisation; Process/fees §§17-22-920–940 (§17-22-920 clerk directs inquiries to solicitor; §17-22-930 mandatory solicitor-office blank order form, to exclusion of other forms; §17-22-940(A) administrative fee $250 per individual order, retained by solicitor’s office, nonrefundable even if later found ineligible or solicitor does not consent; two fees not to be conflated: conditional discharge $350/$150 vs expungement $250); Coastal Law cross-check (“Simple possession: immediately if you completed a conditional discharge. Otherwise, three years from conviction.”; other waiting periods: most 30-day misdemeanors 3 years; CDV third degree 5 years; fraudulent check 1 year; failure to stop for blue light 3 years after completion if no bodily injury; Youthful Offender 5 years after completion); What is NOT expungeable / limits (secondary: traffic incl. DUI/DUAC generally cannot be expunged, exceptions: reckless driving → PTI, DUI re-written as reckless driving in prosecutor’s discretion, failure to stop for blue light 3 years after completion if no bodily injury, minor traffic via TEP dismissal/expungement; second/subsequent possession, distribution/manufacture, trafficking do NOT fit first-offence routes; no broad “all marijuana convictions” expungement law); Pardon separate executive route (Governor / Board of Paroles and Pardons), NOT researched; Proposed expansion H.3730 (2025–2026, “Expungement”): ADD §17-22-915 — (A) first-offence nonviolent offence (§16-1-70) if no pending charges + no other conviction for 10 years from conviction; (B) drug-treatment-court completers (first-offence nonviolent) if no pending charges + no other conviction for 3 years from completion; (C) no more than once; SLED nonpublic record; amends §17-22-910 to reference §17-22-915 and §17-22-940 (court verification of eligibility for drug-treatment-court participants) — “official history/enactment was NOT checked — present as PROPOSED only, do not present §17-22-915 as current law”; No SC “Second Chance Act” marijuana expungement law under that name locatedConfirmed (conditional-discharge fees; PTI listing limb; H.3730 bill text; pardon as a gap); Corrected — MAJOR (§22-5-930 IS current law; §17-22-910 list; fee description; trigger date); Unverified (headline, (B) text, §22-5-910 full text, $250 currency, traffic/PTI-rewrite claims, H.3730 disposition)SC Treasurer Distribution Annual Summary FY 2025–2026 (§44-53-450(C) fees); Title 22, Chapter 5 (current Code, §22-5-930); H.3730 bill text (§17-22-910(A) as reproduced; §17-22-940(D) exists)Keep the headline labelled secondary-supported. MAJOR CORRECTION for Route 3: §22-5-930 IS current law, enacted by 2018 Act No. 254 (H.3209), §4, eff. 27 Dec 2018. Delete the “NOT confirmed current law / Do NOT present H.3209 text as current law” warning for §22-5-930. Correct wording in full: (A) first-offence simple possession under Art. 3, Ch. 53, Title 44, or unlawful possession of a prescription drug under §40-43-86(EE), including charges now eligible for conditional discharge under §44-53-450 — defendant AFTER THREE YEARS FROM THE DATE OF COMPLETION OF THE SENTENCE, INCLUDING PROBATION AND PAROLE (not “three years from conviction” as Run 2 states), including magistrates or general sessions convictions, may apply to circuit court for expungement of arrest/conviction records and any associated bench warrant. (B) first-offence POSSESSION WITH INTENT TO DISTRIBUTE under Art. 3, Ch. 53, Title 44 — after TWENTY YEARS from completion of any sentence (including probation/parole) for a drug or felony conviction — a route Run 2 OMITS entirely; add it. (E) SLED keeps a nonpublic record. §12.5No cannabis-specific landlord/tenant statute; no tenant protection for lawful hemp/CBD use, medical-cannabis housing protection, or landlord right to evict solely for hemp/CBD use located [UNAVAILABLE/VERIFY — Title 27, Chapter 40 was not opened in full]; SC Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Title 27, Chapter 40, §§27-40-10 et seq. (secondary LegalClarity summary); Nonpayment of rent: §27-40-710, landlord can initiate eviction if tenant fails to pay rent on agreed date; grace period not required unless explicitly stated in lease (secondary); Lease violations: §27-40-710(B), if tenant breaches lease — e.g. unauthorised pets, exceeding occupancy limits, damaging property — landlord can seek removal; tenant must be given opportunity to correct within legally required timeframe; if fails, proceedings continue (secondary); Illegal activity on premises: §27-40-740, if tenant engages in criminal conduct such as drug-related offences or violent acts, landlord can terminate lease immediately; unlike other violations, illegal activity does not always require prior notice or opportunity to remedy, especially if it endangers others or property; law enforcement involvement strengthens landlord’s case, though conviction is not necessarily required (secondary, LegalClarity); second secondary (StateRegsToday): landlords must follow proper legal procedures and provide notice before evicting for criminal activity, and tenants may have defences (not involved, landlord had knowledge and failed to act) — secondary conflict on notice for illegal-activity evictions; General tenant-protection summary (StateRegsToday, secondary): landlords have right to terminate/evict for violation of any law/ordinance imposing code restrictions on use/maintenance of property, including criminal activity such as drug-related offences or violent crimes, but must follow proper procedures and provide notice; Lease form language — NOT statute (SC Association of Realtors Form 410; generic month-to-month/standard forms); Proposed bill — PROPOSED only, status not checked: H.4970, 2025–2026, text 15 Jan 2026, ADD §27-40-350 — tenant convicted of crime unrelated to possession, sale, or use of illicit substances or firearms must be given three months to relocate after conviction; if tenant cannot relocate personal property within three-month period, landlord shall store personal property for thirty days; drug/firearm convictions EXCLUDED; Gaps (a)–(e): landlord smoking bans for hemp/CBD smoking/vaping; public/Section 8/federally assisted housing drug rules as applied in SC; landlord drug-testing of tenants; tenant’s right to grow hemp at a rental (SCDA permit requires SC residency, background check, GPS, landlord consent not stated — do not assume it is/is not required); Keep the short title §27-40-10 confirmed. Correct nonpayment to the statute: if rent is unpaid when due and tenant fails to pay within FIVE DAYS from the due date (or tenant violates §27-40-540), landlord may terminate PROVIDED landlord gave written notice of nonpayment + intention to terminate if rent not paid within that period; one such notice (or conspicuous lease language, including the statutory “IF YOU DO NOT PAY YOUR RENT ON TIME…” provision) satisfies the notice duty for later lease terms, including month-to-month holdover. Replace the secondary “grace period not required unless lease states one” phrasing with the 5-day statutory rule. Correct lease-breach citation AND substance: the noncompliance/lease-breach rule is §27-40-710(A), NOT (B) — (B) is nonpayment of rent. Under (A): for noncompliance other than nonpayment or §27-40-510 health/safety or §27-40-540 noncompliance, landlord must deliver written notice specifying the acts/omissions and stating the agreement will terminate on a date NOT LESS THAN 14 DAYS after receipt if the breach is not remedied in 14 days; no termination if the breach is remedied in 14 days, or if remedy is commenced within 14 days and pursued in good faith to completion within a reasonable time. It is NOT an illegal-activity eviction provision. Jay’s Head Shop and Wellness Center LLC), “261 of 270 brands … came back hot” (SLED lab); “40 narcotics charges in initial unsealings” (attributed to Run 1 Part 0); “AG/SLED isomer position” / product “treated as Schedule I under the AG's advisory opinion (not law) and SLED's enforcement position; no SC appellate court holding construing the Hemp Farming Act on delta-8/THCA was located”; THCA / delta-9 / delta-10 / HHC retail status as settled law; GA-vs-SC practical conflict: SC has “no total-THC test” (and no retail licence, no age rule, no COA requirement in current law)Confirmed (statute text as to chapeau + item 18; opinion existence/date/requester/labelling; Cook letter substance/labelling; Ganjapreneur scag-confirmed counts, with qualifier); Corrected (Hemp Farming Act exception wording; “AG/SLED position” labelling; The isomer reading is therefore grounded in the chapeau + item 18, not in a plural “tetrahydrocannabinols” list item. The Hemp Farming Act exception is the §46-55-10(6)/(8) federally defined level (see cross-run row), not a freestanding “delta-9 only” exception sentence. Keep the 2021 AG opinion labelled “OPINION, not law” everywhere. Secondary summaries agree on substance (AG view: Hemp Farming Act does not except/legalise delta-8 or any other THC isomer in itself; only the federally defined delta-9 level is excepted), but the AG PDF itself was not fully retrieved in this audit either — do not quote it verbatim. Minor date note: one secondary source calls it an 8 Oct 2021 letter; the archive date used in the report is 4 Oct 2021 — carry both dates as archive vs letter date until the PDF is opened, do not silently pick one. Keep the Cook letter labelled opinion, not law, and distinct from the 2021 opinion; the scag.gov letter PDF itself was not opened — verbatim letter text beyond the reported quote remains [VERIFY]. Add a date limit: the letter’s delta-9 ≤0.3% test is the pre-PL 119-37 test; after 11 Dec 2026 the federal test becomes total-THC + 0.4 mg/container (baseline), so the 2024 letter cannot be quoted as the current federal test. Keep July 2019 [VERIFY full July 2019 opinion text on scag.gov before quoting]; do not upgrade on the basis of the Speaker Smith paraphrase. Keep Ganjapreneur with the report’s own qualifier: “Allegations/indictments, not convictions.” Enforcement posture is therefore AG/SLED enforcement + indictments, not a court holding that any particular product class is marijuana — do not present Ganjapreneur as a legal ruling on delta-8/THCA. The SCDA total-THC test governs licensed production, not retail sale. Retail THCA/isomer status is an interpretive gap (statute federally defined level vs AG opinion vs Ganjapreneur enforcement) — do not present secondary “THCA is legal at retail in SC” claims as law. PART 2A — CORRECTED REWRITE (PARTS 0–6)

Part 2A is the original Run 1 report with audit corrections applied in place. Every section and detail is retained; only what the audit changed was changed. Clearly-marked [AUDIT CORRECTION] boxes state the corrected wording immediately before the subsection they correct, and the text replacements listed in the merge log were applied throughout. Where a correction could not be applied by a simple text replacement, the box governs over the original text that follows it.

Run 1 — Parts 0–6 only. All facts accessed 24 October 2026 unless a different publication date is stated. Official sources were opened directly where stated; where a fact rests only on a search result, secondary summary, or an unopened official page, it is flagged [VERIFY] or [UNAVAILABLE]. Proposed bills are never presented as law.

Federal baseline used as fixed context (not re-researched): state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); all adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I; IRS 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity and remains fully applicable to adult-use; PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026 but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026, after which the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply; USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026; the federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026; there is no federal cannabis banking law.

Central finding — read first: South Carolina has no state-licensed medical marijuana programme, no adult-use programme, and no state cannabis licence. The only current medical exception is the narrow Julian's Law low-THC/CBD carve-out. Therefore, under the split-scheduling baseline, marijuana remains Schedule I in South Carolina: there is no SC state-licensed medical activity to which the Schedule III move can attach, and SC's own Schedule I list still includes marijuana and THC. Whether the SC Department of Public Health will act under §44-53-160(C) to conform state schedules to the federal change is [VERIFY — no DPH Schedule III conforming update was located].

PART 0: HEADLINES

  1. Legal status: illegal for recreational and for general medical use; low-THC/CBD only, narrowly; hemp (federally defined THC level, §46-55-10(6)/(8)) legal. Marijuana is Schedule I in SC, subject to the Julian's Law exceptions in §44-53-110(27)(b)(v)–(vi) and Article 18, §§44-53-1810–1840. No adult-use or general medical statute exists. SC Code Title 44, Chapter 53; Title 46, Chapter 55. Accessed 2026-10-24.
  2. Hemp is legal only on the federally defined THC level test — for now, in state law. SC hemp uses “a delta-9 THC concentration of not more than 0.3 percent on a dry weight basis, or the THC concentration for hemp defined in 7 U.S.C. SECTION 5940, whichever is greater” (§46-55-10(6)). No total-THC test, no per-container mg cap, and no statewide minimum age for hemp products exist in current SC statute. Title 46, Chapter 55. Accessed 2026-10-24.
  3. Delta-8 / THC isomers: the single biggest legal risk — statute vs. enforcement conflict. The Attorney General's 4 October 2021 opinion (opinion, not law) holds the Hemp Farming Act does not legalise delta-8 or any other THC isomer “in itself” — only delta-9 up to 0.3% is excepted. SLED follows that position. The AG opinion PDF itself was not fully retrieved in this run, so its verbatim holding is [VERIFY] before quoting it as a quotation. AG Opinions Archive, 4 Oct 2021 entry. Accessed 2026-10-24.
  4. Major enforcement: Operation Ganjapreneur. 9 December 2025: State Grand Jury / AG / SLED / DEA searches in the Midlands — 12 defendants arrested, charge count deleted by audit — not in the scag.gov December release; follow-up indictments were for “hundreds of counts”, 6 warehouses, 6 residences, 1 retail business and 2 storage units searched, ~30,000 lb / 15 tons seized, ~$2 million in proceeds/assets seized. Follow-up indictments in March 2026 named Dab City Warehouse, LLC and Jay's Head Shop and Wellness Center LLC; the AG stated SLED lab testing found “261 of the 270 brands of product tested so far from these businesses came back hot.” These are allegations/indictments, not convictions. AG release, Dec 2025; AG release, Mar 2026. Accessed 2026-10-24.
  5. Medical cannabis bill: NOT law; stalled in committee in this session. S.53, Compassionate Care Act, 126th General Assembly (2025–2026), by Davis, Goldfinch and Sutton: prefiled 11 December 2024, introduced and referred to Senate Medical Affairs 14 January 2025, with no further action shown on the official bill page. S.53 official history. Accessed 2026-10-24. Prior-session Senate passage (S.423 in 2024) does not carry this bill into law.
  6. Hemp-regulation bills: H.3924 failed; H.3935/H.4759 were pending as of 24 Oct 2026 — no new state hemp retail law — no new state hemp retail law. H.3924 passed both chambers in amended forms, went to conference, and on 25 June 2026 the House rejected the conference report 28–69 while the Senate adopted it 27–11. H.3924 official history. Accessed 2026-10-24. H.3935 never left House Judiciary; H.4759 was recommitted to House Judiciary 4 February 2026. All are PROPOSED/dead, not law.
  7. Federal hemp cliff with NO SC official response located. No SC Department of Agriculture, DPH, SLED or AG statement responding to PL 119-37 §781 or PL 119-103 §2019, or to the 12 November / 11 December 2026 dates, was found. [UNAVAILABLE as of 2026-10-24]. SC statute still uses the federally defined THC level test (§46-55-10(6)/(8)), so the federal total-THC / 0.4 mg-per-container change would bite in SC by federal operation after 11 December 2026 unless SC or Congress acts — do not present this as a SC state-law change.
  8. Key numbers — conflicting secondary arrest figures, not an official SLED total. NORML/FBI NIBRS table: SC marijuana possession arrests 10,634 in 2025; total marijuana arrests 11,754 in 2025. MPP (7 Oct 2026, also FBI-based): possession 10,352; total 11,446. Difference is likely different FBI reporting cutoffs. Quote neither as an official SLED total; see Research Notes. NORML SC arrests; MPP blog, 7 Oct 2026. Accessed 2026-10-24.
  9. Agency names confirmed. DHEC was dissolved 1 July 2024 into the SC Department of Public Health (DPH, dph.sc.gov) and the SC Department of Environmental Services (SCDES, des.sc.gov). SCDES history. Accessed 2026-10-24.
  10. Hemp programme scale (official, dated). USDA approved SC's Hemp Farming State Plan; SCDA announced approval 2 April 2020. USDA's approved-plan list, updated 17 February 2026, still lists “South Carolina — SC Approved Plan.” SC therefore runs its own USDA-approved state plan, not USDA direct licensing. SCDA, 2 Apr 2020; USDA plan-review list. Accessed 2026-10-24.

PART 1: LAWS

1.1 Legal status

Recreational: illegal. General medical: illegal. Low-THC/CBD only: yes, narrowly (Julian's Law). Hemp meeting the federally defined THC level: legal. Home cultivation of marijuana is prohibited; no statute authorises it. Cultivation is charged as manufacture/production under §44-53-370.

1.2 Every state statute and regulation

A. Title 44, Chapter 53, Article 3 — Narcotics and Controlled Substances

Official link: scstatehouse.gov/code/t44c053.php. Accessed 2026-10-24.

  • §44-53-110(27) — “Marijuana” defined. Verbatim operative part:
    “(27)(a) 'Marijuana' means: (i) all species or variety of the marijuana plant and all parts thereof whether growing or not; (ii) the seeds of the marijuana plant; (iii) the resin extracted from any part of the marijuana plant; or (iv) every compound, manufacture, salt, derivative, mixture, or preparation of the marijuana plant, marijuana seeds, or marijuana resin.”
    “(b) 'Marijuana' does not mean: … (v) for persons participating in a clinical trial or in an expanded access program related to administering cannabidiol for the treatment of severe forms of epilepsy pursuant to Article 18…a drug or substance approved…by the [FDA]; or (vi) for persons, or the persons' parents, legal guardians, or other caretakers, who have received a written certification from a physician licensed in this State that the person has been diagnosed…as having Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome, Dravet Syndrome, also known as 'severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy', or any other severe form of epilepsy that is not adequately treated by traditional medical therapies, the substance cannabidiol, a nonpsychoactive cannabinoid, or any compound…that contains nine-tenths of one percent or less of tetrahydrocannabinol and more than fifteen percent of cannabidiol.”
    Last amendment shown: 2014 Act No. 221 (Julian's Law), eff. 2 June 2014, plus 2026 Act No. 146 agency-name substitution, eff. 15 May 2026.
  • §44-53-110(33) — “Paraphernalia” includes marijuana/hashish pipes, water pipes, bongs, roach clips, etc., but “does not include cigarette papers and tobacco pipes.”
  • §44-53-190(D) — Schedule I. The list as opened includes “11. Marijuana” and “18. Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC).” Last amendment shown: 2023 Act No. 72, eff. 15 June 2023. §44-53-190(D)(24) also lists synthetic cannabinoids as Schedule I.
  • §44-53-160 — Schedule changes. (B) DPH may add/delete/reschedule when the General Assembly is not in session; (C) if a substance is added/deleted/rescheduled under federal law, the DPH Director “shall within thirty days after publication in the federal register of the final order…add, delete, or reschedule the substance in the appropriate schedule.” The Code page directs readers to DPH's schedule page — that page was not opened in this run, so no claim is made about whether DPH has yet posted a Schedule III medical entry. [VERIFY]

B. Title 46, Chapter 55 — The Hemp Farming Act

Official link: scstatehouse.gov/code/t46c055.php. Accessed 2026-10-24. 2014 Act No. 216; rewritten 2017 Act No. 37, eff. 10 May 2017; rewritten 2019 Act No. 14 (H.3449), eff. 28 March 2019 — last amendment shown on the Code page.

  • §46-55-10(6) — “Federally defined THC level for hemp” (verbatim): “a delta-9 THC concentration of not more than 0.3 percent on a dry weight basis, or the THC concentration for hemp defined in 7 U.S.C. SECTION 5940, whichever is greater.”
  • §46-55-10(8) — “Hemp” or “industrial hemp” (verbatim): “the plant Cannabis sativa L. and any part of that plant, including the nonsterilized seeds thereof and all derivatives, extracts, cannabinoids, isomers, acids, salts, and salts of isomers, whether growing or not, with the federally defined THC level for hemp. Hemp shall be considered an agricultural commodity.”
  • §46-55-10(9) — “Hemp products” (verbatim, abridged only by ellipsis): “all products with the federally defined THC level for hemp derived from, or made by, processing hemp plants or hemp plant parts, that are prepared in a form available for commercial sale, including, but not limited to, cosmetics, personal care products, food intended for animal or human consumption, cloth, cordage, fiber, fuel, paint, paper, particleboard, plastics, and any product containing one or more hemp-derived cannabinoids, such as cannabidiol. Unprocessed or raw plant material, including nonsterilized hemp seeds, is not considered a hemp product.”
  • §46-55-10(11): “'Marijuana' has the same meaning as in Section 44-53-110 and does not include tetrahydrocannabinol in hemp or hemp products as defined herein.”
  • §46-55-20(A)(1) — Licence requirement (verbatim): “It is unlawful for a person to cultivate, handle, or process hemp in this State without a hemp license issued by the department pursuant to the state plan.” Fees: cultivators/handlers “shall not exceed one thousand dollars annually per registrant,” processors “shall not exceed the cost calculated by the department.” Background checks: SLED + FBI fingerprint checks; “No person who has been convicted of a felony relating to a controlled substance under state or federal law during a ten-year period from the date of his conviction shall be eligible.”
  • §46-55-30 — Application of chapter (verbatim): “The provisions contained in this chapter do not apply to the possession, handling, transport, or sale of hemp products and extracts, including those containing hemp-derived cannabinoids, including CBD. Nothing in this chapter authorizes any person to violate any federal or state law or regulation.” This is why SC has no state hemp-retail licence, packaging, labelling or buffer regime in Chapter 55.
  • §46-55-40 — Corrective action plans. Negligent violations (including producing Cannabis sativa L. above the federally defined THC level) get a corrective action plan as the sole remedy; three negligent violations in five years = five-year ineligibility; a violation “with a culpable mental state greater than negligence” must be reported to the AG and SLED Chief.
  • §46-55-60 — Unlawful conduct relating to marijuana in proximity to industrial hemp (verbatim, operative): “An individual who manufactures, distributes, dispenses, delivers, purchases, aids, abets, attempts to, or conspires to manufacture, distribute, dispense, deliver, or purchase, or possesses with the intent to manufacture, distribute, dispense, deliver, or purchase marijuana, in a manner intended to disguise the marijuana due to its proximity to industrial hemp, is guilty of a misdemeanor and, upon conviction, must be imprisoned not more than three years, fined not more than three thousand dollars, or both.”
  • Regulations: No SC hemp regulation chapter was verified in this run. [VERIFY — SC Code of Regulations hemp rules, if any under SCDA/state plan, were not opened; the state plan itself is the operative instrument.] SCDA hemp page: agriculture.sc.gov/hemp/. Accessed 2026-10-24.

C. Julian's Law — Article 18, §§44-53-1810–1840

2014 Act No. 221 (S.1035), eff. 2 June 2014; no later substantive amendment shown on the Code page. Official link as in A above.

  • §44-53-1810(3) — “Cannabidiol” for clinical trials (verbatim): “a finished preparation containing, of its total cannabinoid content, at least 98 percent cannabidiol and not more than 0.90 percent tetrahydrocannabinol by volume that has been extracted from marijuana or synthesized in a laboratory.”
  • §44-53-1810(7) — “Qualifying patient” (verbatim): “anyone who suffers from Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome, Dravet Syndrome, also known as severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy, or any other form of refractory epilepsy that is not adequately treated by traditional medical therapies.”
  • §44-53-1820: A statewide investigational new drug application may be established “if approved by the [FDA] to conduct expanded access clinical trials using cannabidiol on qualifying patients”; principal investigator must be a board-certified physician practising at an academic medical centre in SC, FDA-approved as principal investigator, and DEA-licensed.
  • §44-53-1830: Trials “only shall utilize cannabidiol which is: (1) from an approved source; and (2) approved by the [FDA] to be used for treatment of a condition specified in an investigational new drug application.”
  • §44-53-1840 — Immunity: “A person acting in compliance with the provisions of this article must not be subject to arrest, prosecution, or any civil or administrative penalty…for the use, prescription, administration, possession, manufacture, or distribution of medical cannabis.”
  • No registry, no dispensary, no patient card, no purchase system is created by Julian's Law. The patient-side protection in §44-53-110(27)(b)(vi) (≤0.9% THC, >15% CBD, written physician certification) is a definitional exclusion from “marijuana,” not a licensing programme. No out-of-state reciprocity exists in statute [VERIFY — no reciprocity section was found; absence is stated as a search result, not as a quoted prohibition].

D. 1980 Controlled Substances Therapeutic Research Act — Article 4, §§44-53-610–660

1980 Act No. 323; agency name updated 2026 Act No. 146, eff. 15 May 2026. Still in the Code as opened — this must NOT be presented as an operating programme:

§44-53-630(A): “There is established in the Department of Public Health a controlled substances therapeutic research program. The program shall distribute to cancer chemotherapy and radiology patients and to glaucoma patients who are certified pursuant to this article marijuana under the terms and conditions of this article…”

§44-53-650(a): “The director shall obtain marijuana through whatever means he deems most appropriate consistent with federal law.” No operating distribution, patient count, or implementing regulation was located [UNAVAILABLE]; S.53 (2025–2026) would repeal Article 4. Do not cite Article 4 as a usable patient pathway without a Run 2 check of DPH implementation.

AUDIT CORRECTIONS — Paraphernalia and accommodation

§44-53-391 is CONFIRMED on the current scstatehouse.gov Code page (replacing the Run 1 Justia 2022 reproduction): unlawful to advertise, manufacture, possess, sell/deliver, or possess with intent to deliver paraphernalia; civil fine ≤$500 (person) / ≤$50,000 (corporation); 1982 Act No. 400, §2. Added, omitted by Run 1: §44-53-393 (2023 Act No. 72): “drug paraphernalia” does not include rapid fentanyl test strips or fentanyl testing equipment. §44-53-460 accommodation reduction does NOT apply to a controlled substance classified in Schedule I (B) and (C) which is a narcotic drug or LSD, or in Schedule II which is a narcotic drug. §44-53-190(D) history note: 2023 Act No. 72 §1 added item (48) to §44-53-190(B), not to the (D) Schedule I list; §4 of the same Act created §44-53-393. Do not attribute a (D) amendment to Act 72.

1.3 Possession, distribution, trafficking, cultivation, paraphernalia, public consumption, product types

All from §44-53-370, Title 44, Chapter 53. Accessed 2026-10-24. Note the two-track structure: (d)(5) is the marijuana-specific simple-possession track; (d)(2) is the general Schedule I–V track.

Offence (SC)Penalty
Simple possession, ≤28 g / 1 oz marijuana or ≤10 g hashish — §44-53-370(d)(5)Misdemeanor, ≤30 days or $100–$200 fine. Second/subsequent: misdemeanor, ≤1 year or $200–$1,000, or both. Sentence may be suspended/probation granted. Possession of more than 28 g / 1 oz marijuana or 10 g hashish is prima facie a (a) distribution offence.
Simple possession, other Schedule I–V (general) — §44-53-370(d)(2)First: misdemeanor, ≤6 months or ≤$1,000, or both. Second/subsequent: misdemeanor, ≤1 year or ≤$2,000, or both. This track would cover a non-marijuana THC product charged as a Schedule I substance other than marijuana — the charging theory SLED/AG use for isomer products — but the charging decision itself is [VERIFY — no charging guidance was opened].
Possession with intent / manufacture / distribution — §44-53-370(a)–(b)(2)First: felony, ≤5 years or ≤$5,000, or both. Second: felony, ≤10 years or ≤$10,000, or both. Third/subsequent: felony, 5–20 years or ≤$20,000, or both. First/second sentences may be suspended/probation granted; third/subsequent generally may not, except where all priors were (c)/(d) possession.
Trafficking in marijuana — §44-53-370(e)(1) (10 lbs+)10–<100 lbs, first: 1–10 years, no suspension/probation, $10,000 fine. Second: 5–20 years, $15,000. Third/subsequent: mandatory 25 years, $25,000. 100–<2,000 lbs or 100–1,000 plants: mandatory 25 years, $25,000. 2,000–<10,000 lbs or >1,000–<10,000 plants: mandatory 25 years, $50,000. 10,000+ lbs or 10,000+ plants: 25–30 years, mandatory minimum 25 years, $200,000. Mandatory-25-year sentences: no parole, extended work release, or supervised furlough. Weight includes pure form or any compound/mixture.
CultivationNo separate home-grow offence: cultivation is “manufacture” / “production” (§44-53-110(37): “Production includes the manufacture, planting, cultivation, growing, or harvesting of a controlled substance”) and is charged under (a)/(b) above, or as trafficking by plant count under (e)(1).
Conditional discharge / diversion — §44-53-450(A) A person with no prior conviction under this article or any state/federal marijuana/stimulant/depressant/hallucinogenic statute, who pleads/found guilty of possession under §44-53-370(c)–(d) or §44-53-375(A), may, with consent and without entering judgment of guilt, be placed on probation (including treatment/rehabilitation if available); on fulfilment “the court shall discharge the person and dismiss the proceedings” — not a conviction, but a nonpublic record is retained by SLED for later prior-offence determinations; discharge/dismissal “may occur only once.” (B) On dismissal, the person may apply for expungement of all official records (other than that nonpublic record). (C) Fee: $350 in general sessions court, $150 in summary court, waivable/reducible only for indigency. Last amendment shown: 2010 Act No. 273, eff. 2 June 2010.
Accommodation reduction — §44-53-460A person convicted under (a) or (c) who proves by clear and convincing evidence delivery/possession with intent was “only as an accommodation to another individual and not with intent to profit” (and not to induce use/dependence) “shall [be sentenced] as if he had been convicted of a violation of Section 44-53-370(c)” — i.e. as simple possession.
Paraphernalia — §44-53-391Secondary summaries of the official text agree: unlawful to advertise, manufacture, possess, sell/deliver, or possess with intent to sell/deliver paraphernalia; violation is a civil fine of not more than $500 for a person, not more than $50,000 for a corporation, and “shall not give rise to any disability or legal disadvantage based on conviction for a criminal offense.” [VERIFY — §44-53-391 was not opened on scstatehouse.gov in this run; confirm verbatim text there before relying on it.] Source for secondary text: current scstatehouse.gov Code page. Accessed 2026-10-24.
Public consumptionNo standalone SC public-consumption offence for marijuana was located in Chapter 53 in this run [VERIFY/UNAVAILABLE]. Public use would in practice be charged as possession (§44-53-370(c)–(d)) and/or under local ordinances — do not invent a public-consumption penalty.
Product types — what is legal?Flower, edibles, vapes, concentrates and beverages made from marijuana are all illegal (no product-type authorisation exists; “marijuana” covers every compound/preparation). The only lawful product categories are: (i) hemp products meeting §46-55-10(9) (including CBD products), subject to the delta-8/isomer enforcement conflict; (ii) Julian's Law CBD preparations meeting §44-53-110(27)(b)(vi) or §44-53-1810(3); (iii) FDA-approved products under federal law. Smokable hemp flower: not a “hemp product” if it is unprocessed/raw plant material (§46-55-10(9) exclusion) — its retail status is therefore contested and is a focus of SLED enforcement; no statute expressly bans or expressly authorises retail smokable flower [VERIFY — interpretive gap, do not resolve it here].

1.4 Medical — Julian's Law summary

Qualifies: Lennox-Gastaut, Dravet, or other refractory epilepsy not adequately treated by traditional therapies. THC/CBD limits — two different standards, do not conflate them: (a) definitional exclusion (§44-53-110(27)(b)(vi)): ≤0.9% THC and >15% CBD, with written physician certification (physician protected from detrimental action for giving it); (b) clinical-trial preparation (§44-53-1810(3)): ≥98% CBD of total cannabinoid content and ≤0.90% THC by volume, from an FDA-approved source, via a board-certified academic-medical-centre physician as FDA principal investigator. Agency: no registry agency — trials run through academic medical centres + FDA/DEA; the definitional exclusion is self-executing on certification, with no state card or dispensary. No broader medical programme, no reciprocity.

AUDIT CORRECTION — Hemp definition (applies everywhere in Part 2A)

Do not use the unqualified delta-9 shorthand. Hemp is defined by the federally defined THC level, §46-55-10(6)/(8): a delta-9 THC concentration of not more than 0.3% on a dry weight basis, or the THC concentration for hemp defined in 7 U.S.C. §5940, whichever is greater. For licensed production, SCDA programme material applies a post-decarboxylation total-THC ≤0.3% test (§46-55-20(B)(2)(b) consent). Chapter 55 does not govern finished hemp products (§46-55-30). The federal total-THC definition and 0.4 mg per container cap apply by federal operation after 11 December 2026 (baseline), not as SC state law. The AG delta-8 position is an advisory opinion, not law; SLED's position is an enforcement position. No SC appellate court holding construing the Hemp Farming Act on delta-8/THCA was located. AG opinion date and verbatim holding remain [VERIFY] (archive entry and SLED Chief Keel as requester confirmed; a secondary source also gives an 8 October 2021 letter date). THCA / delta-10 / HHC finished-product retail status and smokable hemp flower retail status remain interpretive gaps — §46-55-10(9) states: “Unprocessed or raw plant material, including nonsterilized hemp seeds, is not considered a hemp product.”

1.5 Hemp: THC measurement, delta-8/delta-9/THCA, AG/SLED positions, drinks/edibles, age, retail licensing, testing/labelling, federal response

  • Measurement: Delta-9 THC concentration on a dry-weight basis, post-decarboxylation or similarly reliable methods for licensed production (state plan; §46-55-20(B)(2)(b) consent to that testing procedure). No total-THC (THC + THCA×0.877) formula appears in Chapter 55 [VERIFY — formula, if any, would be in the state plan/regulations, not opened].
  • Delta-9: ≤0.3% dry weight = hemp. Above = marijuana.
  • Delta-8 / delta-10 / HHC / THCA / synthetics: Statute says hemp includes “isomers” (§46-55-10(8)), which is the industry's textual argument; the AG's 4 Oct 2021 opinion (OPINION, not law) rejects it, holding only delta-9 is excepted. SCDA hemp programme guidance is reported to repeat that position [VERIFY — SCDA delta-8 guidance page was not opened]. THCA: no SC statute separately regulates THCA; under the federally defined THC level test (§46-55-10(6)/(8)), THCA flower testing at or below the federally defined THC level is treated by retailers as hemp, while SLED/AG treat high-THCA product sold as marijuana as marijuana — an unresolved enforcement conflict, not settled law.
  • THC drinks and edibles: No current SC statute caps mg/serving or mg/package, bans, or licenses hemp drinks/edibles for retail. The failed 2025–2026 bills would have done so (see §1.9). General food law may apply to ingestibles [VERIFY — no SCDA/DPH food guidance for hemp edibles was opened].
  • Minimum age: None in current SC statute for hemp/CBD/THC products. Retailer 18+/21+ policies are voluntary. All pending 2025–2026 hemp bills proposed 21+ — PROPOSED only.
  • Retail licensing/registration: None at state level for hemp/CBD retail (Chapter 55 expressly does not apply to sale of hemp products, §46-55-30). General SC retail licence / sales-tax registration with DOR applies to any retailer (see Part 2), plus local business licences (Part 3).
  • Testing/labelling for retail products: No state testing or labelling rule for retail hemp/CBD products was located in Chapter 55 [UNAVAILABLE]. Licensed cultivation is sampled/tested pre-harvest under the state plan (SCDA 2020 release: “SCDA staff sample every hemp field in the state prior to harvest”).
  • State response to new federal hemp definition: None found [UNAVAILABLE] — see Part 0.7. Note the drafting trap: several failed SC bills already used a 0.4 mg total THC per container cap (mirroring the federal cap) — that cap is PROPOSED, not current SC law, and must not be quoted as SC law.

1.6 Packaging, labelling, advertising, delivery, zoning/buffers — hemp/CBD and smoke/vape shops

Current SC law: no hemp/CBD-specific packaging, labelling, advertising, delivery, zoning or buffer statute was located. Chapter 55 contains none (see §46-55-30). Therefore: packaging/labelling governed only by general law (food, consumer protection, federal FDA/FTC) [VERIFY — no SC-specific rule opened; do not invent one]; advertising: no hemp-specific restriction in statute [VERIFY]; delivery: no hemp-specific delivery ban or licence in current law — failed bill versions proposed banning online/direct shipment of consumable hemp products, PROPOSED only, not law; zoning/buffers for hemp/CBD/smoke/vape shops: no statewide buffer for hemp retail in current law. The 1,000-ft school buffer in S.53 §44-53-2410(B)(5)(a) is PROPOSED for medical establishments only. Local zoning/business-licence rules are Part 3.

Contrast — proposed (not law) packaging/labelling in failed bills: H.3935 summaries (secondary): 21+, behind-counter, school-proximity limits, youth-oriented packaging/advertising bars, independent-lab testing, detailed labelling/warnings, potency limits for ingestibles/inhalables in amendments. [VERIFY against official bill text before quoting any mg figure as a proposal detail.]

1.7 Seed-to-sale / product tracking

None for hemp/CBD retail. For licensed hemp cultivation, the state plan requires land legal description + GPS coordinates (§46-55-20(B)(1)), law-enforcement real-time access to licensee/land information (§46-55-20(A)(5)), and pre-harvest sampling — that is plot registration and compliance sampling, not a Metrc-style seed-to-sale system. No tracking system is named in Chapter 55. No medical seed-to-sale system exists because no medical programme exists. S.53 would have required pharmacy-level tracking/reporting — PROPOSED only.

1.9 Pending legislation — scstatehouse.gov status, two-year session rule

Two-year session rule: SC General Assembly operates on a two-year cycle. Bills carry over from year 1 to year 2 of the same General Assembly, but bills that do not pass by the end of the second year die and must be refiled in the next General Assembly. Secondary explainer (SCETV, 26 Jan 2026): “Bills that don't cross the finish line by the end of the second year don't carry over—they expire.” SCETV explainer. Accessed 2026-10-24. Consequence: every 126th General Assembly (2025–2026) bill below that did not become law is dead at the end of the 126th session and would need refiling in the 127th (2027–2028) — it is NOT “pending” into 2027 unless refiled. The 126th session's extended activity in June 2026, including the 25 June conference votes, is already reflected below; do not assume further 2026 action without checking the journals.

PART 2: TAXES

AUDIT CORRECTIONS — Sales/use tax pinpoints and unprepared food

§12-36-910 imposes 5%; §12-36-1110 adds 1% = 6% state sales tax. §12-36-1310(A) imposes a 5% use tax (6% combined with the additional 1%) — do not write that §12-36-1310(A) itself imposes 6%. Unprepared food is NOT exempt from SC sales tax: it is excluded only from the additional 1% under §12-36-1110, so it is taxed at 5% state (unless another §12-36-2120 exemption covers it). Ordinary over-the-counter CBD/hemp retail products are not “medicine sold by prescription” under §12-36-2120(28)(a). No DOR ruling specifically on CBD/hemp taxability was opened [VERIFY].

2.1 State sales and use tax on hemp/CBD/THC products — current law

  • Rate: 6% state. S.C. Code §12-36-910(A) imposes sales tax on gross proceeds of retail sales of tangible personal property (§12-36-910 is a 5% base; §12-36-1110 adds 1%, for an effective 6%). §12-36-1310(A) imposes a 5% use tax (6% combined with the additional 1% under §12-36-1110). DOR's restatement: “A sales tax, equal to [six] percent of the gross proceeds of sales, is imposed upon every person engaged or continuing within this State in the business of selling tangible personal property at retail.” DOR Policy Manual Ch. 7. Accessed 2026-10-24. [Note: this DOR manual was reached via search result text, not a browser.open page read in this run — confirm the live DOR page before relying on it.]
  • Application to hemp/CBD: Hemp/CBD products sold at retail are tangible personal property; no hemp/CBD-specific sales-tax exemption exists in §12-36-2120 as verified in this run — so retail hemp/CBD sales are taxable at 6% state (+ local, below), subject to any generally applicable exemption (e.g. medicine sold by prescription under §12-36-2120(28)(a) — ordinary CBD/hemp retail products are not covered; unprepared food purchasable with USDA food coupons is taxed at 5% state, not 6%, because the additional 1% does not apply to it). [VERIFY — no DOR ruling specifically on CBD/hemp taxability was opened; the conclusion follows from the general tangible-property rule, not from a CBD-specific ruling.]
  • Retail licence: A retailer must obtain a DOR retail licence and collect/remit (general rule, §12-36-1340 framework, per DOR manual above). This is a tax registration, NOT a cannabis/hemp licence.
  • No cannabis sales-tax revenue figure exists because there is no lawful cannabis market to tax. No official hemp/CBD sales-tax revenue breakout was located [UNAVAILABLE].

2.2 Hemp-specific excise or licence tax — current law

None. No hemp excise tax, no per-ounce/per-mg tax, and no hemp-retail licence tax exists in current SC statute. The only hemp fees in current law are SCDA cultivation/handler/processor licence fees capped as in §46-55-20(A)(2) (cultivators/handlers ≤$1,000/year per registrant; processors at department-calculated cost) — see Part 1.2B. Proposed (NOT law): H.3924 versions: per-ounce wholesale tax + biennial licence taxes above; H.3935: 2% retail excise (secondary summary). Both died/failed — see §1.9.

SC conformity is through 31 December 2024 (2025 Act No. 63); DOR IL26-4 (Revised, 30 January 2026) confirms that date. “Updated annually” is a practice description, not a guarantee. H.3368 is RESOLVED as failed (passed House 10 March 2026, 121–0; failed Senate second reading 31 March 2026, 16–27) — it did not enact a 2025 conformity update. A separate 2025-update proposal, H.5167, remains enactment-unconfirmed. No DOR ruling on 280E was opened; SC treatment of any federal 280E change after the 28 April 2026 rule remains [UNVERIFIED — confirm with DOR]. Do not present SC as giving 280E relief for Schedule III medical activity. Treasury qualifier: rescheduling generally removes 280E as a bar for businesses no longer dealing in Schedule I/II substances, guidance forthcoming. S.53's tax section remains [VERIFY] — do not quote a 6% (or any) medical-cannabis tax rate for the 2025–2026 S.53 from a predecessor bill's fiscal note.

2.4 IRS §280E as it applies in South Carolina — conformity / decoupling

  • SC has NO 280E decoupling statute. SC conforms to the Internal Revenue Code on a fixed-date (static) basis under §12-6-40, updated by the General Assembly (last confirmed: 2025 Act No. 63; no 2026 conformity act confirmed — H.3368 failed 31 Mar 2026). Most recent conformity act opened in this run: S.507, Act No. 63 (2025), updating §12-6-40 to the IRC as amended through 31 Dec 2024, eff. 22 May 2025. DOR Information Letter #26-4 (Revised), 30 Jan 2026, confirms: “South Carolina has conformed with the Internal Revenue Code as amended through December 31, 2024” and had not yet addressed 2025 federal changes. DOR IL26-4 (Revised). Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • Consequence (analytical, not a DOR ruling): Because SC starts from federal taxable income with no 280E add-back/decoupling provision, a business subject to federal §280E would, on the conformity position as of 31 Dec 2024, also be denied those deductions for SC income tax. Secondary tax analysis to the same effect: “South Carolina conforms to the Internal Revenue Code. There is no provision that states Section 280E does not apply.” [VERIFY — no DOR ruling on 280E was opened; and the 2026 conformity bill (H.3368, referenced in secondary coverage as pending in 2026) was not checked — its status and whether it advances conformity past the federal Schedule III rule must be confirmed before any claim about SC treatment of Schedule III medical activity in tax year 2026.]
  • Interaction with the federal split schedule: Federally, 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity and remains fully applicable to adult-use (Schedule I) activity, per the baseline. In SC, that federal lift has no practical in-state taxpayer today (no state-licensed medical programme, no lawful adult-use market); the only SC taxpayers potentially affected are lawful hemp businesses (not subject to 280E, as hemp is not a Schedule I/II controlled substance federally) and any out-of-state activity — do not present SC as having a medical-cannabis 280E benefit.
  • Proposed medical tax in S.53: An earlier-session fiscal note for a predecessor Compassionate Care Act estimated a 6% sales tax on medical cannabis products; whether the 2025–2026 S.53 text itself imposes that tax was not verified in this run [VERIFY — search S.53 text for its tax section before quoting]. Do not quote a medical-cannabis tax rate for S.53 without that check.

PART 3: LOCAL RULES

3.1 Authority: who does what

State level — no state cannabis licence, no state hemp-retail licence (see Part 4). The state regulates hemp production, handling and processing through SCDA under §§46-55-10 et seq., and taxes/retail registration through SCDOR. It does not issue a general state licence for a hemp/CBD/smoke/vape shop.

Local level — zoning and business licences. Under the SC Local Government Comprehensive Planning Enabling Act, Title 6, Chapter 29: §6-29-720(A): “When the local planning commission has prepared and recommended and the governing body has adopted at least the land use element of the comprehensive plan… the governing body of a municipality or county may adopt a zoning ordinance… Within each district the governing body may regulate: (1) the use of buildings, structures, and land…” §6-29-330 (summarised in search result): a municipality exercises Chapter 29 powers inside its corporate limits; a county exercises them in the unincorporated area. This is why the same shop can be subject to city rules, county rules, or both depending on whether it sits inside a city limit.

Business-licence tax: §§6-1-400 et seq. (2020 Act No. 176, Business License Tax Standardization). §6-1-400(A)(1): “Unless otherwise specifically provided for by state law, a county or municipality that levies a business license tax must comply with the provisions of this article.” A business licence is for “the privilege of doing business in that county or municipality,” runs 1 May–30 April, and is computed on gross income, not a flat hemp-specific fee.

PART 4: LICENCE TYPES

4.1 State cannabis licences: NONE — confirmed

South Carolina issues NO cannabis licences. There is no state-licensed medical marijuana programme, no adult-use programme, no cannabis cultivation, processing, dispensary/pharmacy, testing or transporter licence in current law. The only medical-cannabis-adjacent law is Julian's Law (§§44-53-1810 et seq., low-THC CBD for severe epilepsy — Part 1), which creates no dispensary licence. Any “SC dispensary licence” claim is false. Myrtle Beach's zoning text mentioning “medical marijuana dispensaries” (§1313, Part 3) is a zoning category, not a state licence.

January 2027 fee [VERIFY] (no 2027 schedule published while applications are closed; farming applications closed until January 2027). Permits expire annually. Weighmaster: Code §§39-11-30/39-11-60 give $5 / 3 years for public weighmasters, but no SCDA hemp-specific form/fee was located — do NOT present $5 as the confirmed hemp fee [VERIFY with SCDA]. No retail licence exists (handler/processor refusal wording) — a permit non-existence claim, not a claim that retail sale is licensed or banned (§46-55-30 carves hemp products out of Chapter 55). 4.2 Current hemp permits — SCDA, under the Hemp Farming Act (§§46-55-10 et seq.)

Regulator: SCDA, Consumer Protection Division, Hemp Farming Program. Hub page (opened): “SCDA is the regulatory department charged with administering the South Carolina Hemp Farming Program as authorized by SC Code Ann. 46-55-10 et seq. and the SC State Plan… requirements for hemp permitting include a criminal background check, South Carolina residency, and an application fee.” SCDA Hemp Farming Program. Accessed 2026-10-24. Contact on the applications page: 803-734-8339 (public SCDA contact, not a personal number).

Statutory basis: §46-55-20(A)(1): “It is unlawful for a person to cultivate, handle, or process hemp in this State without a hemp license issued by the department pursuant to the state plan.” §46-55-20(A)(2): cultivator/handler fees “shall not exceed one thousand dollars annually per registrant”; processor fees “shall not exceed the cost calculated by the department.” §46-55-20(A)(3): SLED + FBI fingerprint criminal-records checks; “No person who has been convicted of a felony relating to a controlled substance under state or federal law during a ten-year period from the date of his conviction shall be eligible.”

Applications page (opened 2026-10-24): SCDA Hemp Applications.

SCDA states expressly (applications page, opened): “A Handler Permit will not be issued to Retail Operation (including online sales) or Retail Stores” and “SCDA will not issue permits to applicants who only intend to operate retail outlets.” A shop selling finished hemp/CBD products needs only (a) a local business licence, (b) a SCDOR Retail License if making taxable retail sales, and (c) compliance with zoning — no SCDA retail permit. This is the single most important Part 4 correction to any claim that SC “licenses CBD retailers.”N/ASee Part 5 for the (non-existent) retailer list.

Fee conflict to carry into Research Notes: Farmer Permit RESOLVED: $100 application + $500 permit (2024 schedule); $1,000 is the statutory cap / historical 2021 figure, not current. Processor $1,500 is consistent across both eras; the older $3,000 processor figure in some secondary material is superseded by the current $1,500 on the live SCDA page and must not be used. Handler fees are consistent ($250 / $500 by category).

Sampling/testing fees (official, 2024 schedule, for context): Inspector visit $10; non-SCDA PPE visit $25; per-sample $10; resample $15; farmer pays shipping; acreage-amendment/site-modification $50. HempFeeReportingSchedule2024.pdf. Accessed 2026-10-24.
