The $500 producer / $250-per-retail-location scheme (with 10-year felony ineligibility, inspection consent, civil penalties ≤$1,000/violation, 1-year licence) is S.137 §46-56-60 (companion H.3601; S.137 referred to Senate Agriculture and Natural Resources, no further action shown) — delete it as an H.3924 claim. H.3924's own proposed fees are the Title 61 fiscal-note figures ($50,000 manufacturer / $20,000 wholesaler / $1,200 retailer + $100 filing), PROPOSED only. S.53: no dedicated social-equity programme in the text opened; the ≥2-year/≥50%-resident extra-points and African American community board-seat details are S.423-era secondary only, S.53 text [VERIFY]. The secondary claim that the Act “prioritizes minority-owned businesses / financial assistance for low-income individuals” is Unverified — do not use. H.3924 equity absence [VERIFY]. No current social-equity programme exists (negative finding, confirmed). No official startup-cost estimate exists (negative finding, confirmed). Franchise (Carolina Hemp Company), CBDistillery generic ranges, FinModelsLab model and Clemson $6,000–$27,000/acre (2019-era) figures are all Unverified, secondary, dated — keep labelled NON-OFFICIAL.

4.3 PROPOSED licence types — pending medical cannabis bill ONLY (all PROPOSED, none enacted)

S.53, Session 126 (2025–2026), “South Carolina Compassionate Care Act,” Sens. Davis, Goldfinch and Sutton — PROPOSED, NOT LAW. Official bill page (opened): prefiled 11 Dec 2024, referred to Senate Committee on Medical Affairs 11 Dec 2024, introduced/read first time and referred to Medical Affairs 14 Jan 2025. No further action is shown on the official bill page as accessed 2026-10-24. It has not passed the Senate in this session, has not passed the House, and has not been signed. S.53 bill page. PROPOSED caps (corroborated across bill-text search result and MPP summaries, but full text should be re-opened for verbatim quotation): 15 cultivation centre licences; 30 processing facility licences; therapeutic cannabis pharmacies: 1 per 20 pharmacies statewide (≈65), max 3 per county; 5 independent testing laboratory licences; 4 transporter licences; integrated operator licences in the number recommended by the commission, with one licence deducted per function performed; any number of qualifying research facilities meeting department requirements. Merit-based scored application; regulator would be DPH + Board of Pharmacy; seed-to-sale tracking, security, packaging/labelling and advertising rules to be set by regulation; no smoking, no raw flower/leaf; 14-day supply limits.

Session-cycle note: SC runs two-year sessions (Session 126 = 2025–2026). A bill that does not pass both chambers and receive the Governor's signature by sine die dies and must be reintroduced in the next session. S.53's official history shows no action after Jan 2025; secondary MPP material (Oct 2026) states Sen. Davis “is expected [to] reintroduce similar legislation in 2027” — consistent with S.53 dying at the end of Session 126, but the sine-die disposition itself is [VERIFY] on scstatehouse.gov before the final report states it as dead rather than merely stalled in committee.

PROPOSED hemp-retailer/producer licences — H.3924 (2025–2026), “hemp-derived consumables,” NOT ENACTED (FAILED 25 June 2026). Official history: House second reading 9 April 2025 (102–2), third reading 10 April 2025; Senate amended/passed Mar 2026; conference committee appointed 30 Apr 2026; 25 June 2026: House rejected the conference report 28–69; Senate adopted it 27–11 the same day. The bill therefore did NOT become law. PROPOSED (in various versions of H.3924 / Ch. 56 drafts): a person/entity manufacturing or selling hemp-derived-cannabinoid products, “including as a producer or retailer, must obtain a license from the Department of Agriculture,” fee $500 for producers, $250 per retailer per location, 1-year licence renewable annually at the same fee, ineligibility while serving / for 10 years after a drug-related felony sentence, consent to inspection/sampling, civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation. These fees are PROPOSED ONLY and must not be quoted as current fees. The conference version's other reported terms (0.4 mg total THC per container concept, age-21, liquor-outlet-only retail in the compromise) are from secondary reporting of the conference report — [VERIFY] against the 25 June 2026 conference report text before quoting them, and in any case they are dead proposals.

4.4 Social equity

  • Current programme: NONE. South Carolina has no legal cannabis industry and no social-equity programme for cannabis or hemp. No SCDA hemp-permit preference, fee reduction, or set-aside for minority-owned, women-owned, veteran-owned or justice-impacted applicants was located in §§46-55-10 et seq. or on SCDA's hemp pages.
  • Proposed (S.53): NO dedicated social-equity licensing programme located. The bill summaries reviewed describe a merit-based scored process (location, background/qualifications, business and security plans; extra points for ≥2 years operating an SC agricultural/production/manufacturing business or ≥50% SC-resident principals in earlier versions) and a Medical Cannabis Advisory Board that includes “a representative of the African American community” — that board seat is not a social-equity licence programme and must not be described as one. A secondary site's claim that the Compassionate Care Act “prioritiz[es] license applications from minority-owned businesses and offer[s] financial assistance for low-income individuals” was not corroborated in the bill summaries or bill-text extracts reviewed and is treated here as [VERIFY — do not use without the bill text].
  • H.3924 (hemp): no social-equity provision was located in the versions/summaries reviewed [VERIFY].

4.5 Estimated startup costs — NO official SC estimate exists; non-official figures only

No SCDA, SCDOR or other SC official source publishes a hemp-retail or hemp-manufacturing startup-cost estimate. The only figures that can be stated officially are the permit/licence fees in §4.2 plus the generally applicable costs below. Everything else in this subsection is NON-OFFICIAL and must be labelled as such:

  • Official, quantifiable SC costs: Hemp Processor $100 + $1,500/location; Handler $100 + $250/$500 by category; Farmer $100 + $500 (2024 schedule; conflict RESOLVED — see §4.2 box) or $1,000 (older) — plus $50 SCDOR Retail License per location (CONFIRMED on dor.sc.gov), plus local business-licence tax (gross-income based, §3.5), plus SCDA sampling fees ($10/sample etc.).
  • NON-OFFICIAL, national/franchise figures (do NOT present as SC costs): Carolina Hemp Company (franchise, operates in SC among other states): “at least $40,000 in liquid capital,” franchise fee $24,900, “Low Start-Up Investment $60–$100K” (Franchise Gator listing, accessed via search). Generic CBD-retail guide (CBDistillery, undated in extract): initial inventory $10,000–$50,000; licensing/permits $500–$5,000; legal $2,000–$10,000; insurance $2,000–$8,000/yr; POS $1,000–$3,000; buildout $5,000–$50,000; marketing $3,000–$15,000; working capital $10,000–$30,000; “Total startup investment ranges from $50,000 to $250,000.” A modelled CBD-store P&L (FinModelsLab): $340k minimum cash need / $1.135m CAPEX — a generic model, not SC-specific, and its lease ($4,500/mo) and payroll assumptions should not be imported as SC figures.
  • SC-specific cost signal (dated, secondary): Clemson Extension (via Specialty Crop Grower, 2019-era): hemp-for-CBD growers “may be spending anywhere from $6,000 to $27,000 per acre” in variable costs — historical, pre-2020-plan, and not a retail/manufacturing startup estimate. Do not use it as a current figure.

5.4 SLED enforcement data — no licence database

No SLED public database of hemp licensees, retailers, or enforcement actions by business was located. SLED's role in hemp is (a) fingerprint background checks under §46-55-20(A)(3), (b) lab testing of seized product, and (c) enforcement with the AG and local agencies. Usable enforcement source (official, dated): SC Attorney General press release, Operation “Ganjapreneur” — State Grand Jury indictments following 9 Dec 2025 searches/seizures of Midlands distributorships and vape shops: “approximately 30,000 pounds, or 15 tons, of allegedly illegal product” seized in the Midlands; “261 of the 270 brands of product tested so far from these businesses came back hot” (SLED lab testing, per AG Wilson); indictments focused on Dab City Warehouse, LLC and Jay's Head Shop and Wellness Center LLC (operators named in the release). Format: HTML press release, no dataset, no download, no searchable enforcement database. Secondary reporting adds: 12 arrests, ~$2m proceeds seized, 40 drug charges (Dec 2025 round) — use the AG release as the primary citation, secondary figures only if needed and labelled as such. Limitation: enforcement releases name targets, not the licensed population, and must not be used to estimate how many shops exist.

No public Julian's Law patient registry, dispensary list, or official patient count was located. The statute (§§44-53-1810 et seq.) is a clinical/research authorisation, not a retail registry. One secondary patient-advocacy page lists “0 registered patients / 0 retail locations” for SC — that reflects no programme, not a counted zero, and is not adopted here as an official count. Finding for Part 5: counts = [UNAVAILABLE]. Recommended follow-up: SC Department of Public Health (DPH, successor to DHEC for this function — confirm current holder) and MUSC — neither was found to publish a Julian's Law count. Do not state a number.

5.6 SC Secretary of State — Business Entities Online

Official page: sos.sc.gov/online-filings/business-entities/file-and-search-online — “The Business Entities Online system allows users to file corporate documents online and to search entities on file with the Secretary of State's Office. The public may access general information for all entities on file, including registered agent and registered office information. The online system also includes the option of searching for a particular registered agent…” Search portal (from secondary guides corroborating the SOS link structure): businessfilings.sc.gov/businessfiling/Entity/Search — URL to be confirmed by opening it in a live browser; it is given here as the portal path cited by multiple guides, not as a text-extracted official link. Holder type: All SC corporations/LLCs/partnerships etc. on file — not hemp-specific. There is no NAICS, hemp, CBD, or licence-type filter stated. Format: Interactive search page only — no bulk download, no CSV/XLSX export found. Search by entity name (“begins with / contains / exact match”) or by registered agent. Per-entity record shows name, entity ID, type, status, formation date, registered agent/office, filing history; certified documents can be ordered. Access: free, no account required for basic search. Update frequency / latest date: live filing system (continuous) — no “as of” date is published for search results. Fields available: entity name, ID, type, status, formation date, registered agent, registered office. Not available: owners/officers (no officer search), business activity/NAICS, hemp-permit status, or shop addresses beyond the registered office. Limitations (critical): Sole proprietorships and general partnerships do not file with the SOS and will not appear — a large share of small CBD/smoke shops may therefore be invisible here. A SOS hit proves only that an entity exists; it proves nothing about hemp permitting, and a SOS miss proves nothing about whether a shop trades.

5.8 Local (county/city/town) business-licence records

  • No checked jurisdiction publishes a searchable, hemp/CBD-filtered business-licence list. What exists is: general business-licence application and rate-schedule pages (e.g. Summerville Appendix A, Mount Pleasant Appendix A, Lexington Ch. 111 — §3.5), which show how a licence is priced, not who holds one; city/county online portals (e.g. Charleston, Columbia, North Charleston customer portals) for applying/paying for a licence — whether any of them offers a public “search licences” function, and whether any exports a list, is [VERIFY — jurisdiction by jurisdiction, in a live browser]; none was confirmed in text searches for this part; zoning/BZA records (Columbia, Charleston, Charleston County) are public meeting documents that incidentally name individual vape-shop applicants — these are case records, not a licence roster, and must not be compiled into a de facto list without a warning that they are incomplete and anecdotal.
  • Local record-keeping limitation (statutory): §6-1-120 makes business-licence taxpayer information confidential and not subject to FOIA disclosure to third parties (including contingency-fee auditors). That is a further reason not to expect a published local licensee list with gross-income data.

PART 7: HEMP LICENCES

7.1 Regulator and plan status — no switch to USDA-direct licensing

  • Regulator: South Carolina Department of Agriculture (SCDA), Consumer Protection Division, Hemp Farming Program, administering the programme “as authorized by SC Code Ann. 46-55-10 et seq. and the SC State Plan.” Public contact on the applications page: 803-734-8339. SCDA Hemp Farming Program; SCDA Hemp Applications. Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • Own USDA-approved state plan, not USDA-direct licensing — confirmed, no change found: SCDA announced USDA approval of SC's Hemp Farming State Plan on 2 April 2020, the same day the 2020 farming-permit application period ended; the release states the plan “will end an era of regulatory flux,” establishes new reporting/sampling requirements, and mandates SCDA staff sample every hemp field prior to harvest. USDA's approved-plan list, updated 17 February 2026, still lists “South Carolina | SC Approved Plan (pdf).” No later switch to USDA-direct licensing was found. SCDA, 2 Apr 2020; USDA plan-review list; State Plan PDF (2021 amended version retrieved via USDA): SouthCarolinaHempStatePlan.pdf. Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • Date of the change that matters: the operative change is April 2020 — from the 2018 pilot / pre-plan era to the USDA-approved State Plan. The 2018 pilot (20 farmers, university-partner model) and its 40-permit cap, $50 application fee, and university-partnership requirement are superseded pilot-era material and must not be carried forward as current requirements.
  • Statutory basis (Run 1, unchanged): §46-55-20(A)(1): “It is unlawful for a person to cultivate, handle, or process hemp in this State without a hemp license issued by the department pursuant to the state plan.” §46-55-20(A)(2): cultivator/handler licence fees “shall not exceed one thousand dollars annually per registrant”; processor fees “shall not exceed the cost calculated by the department of the processor licensing program.” Title 46, Chapter 55. Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • Method limitation for Part 7/11 — SUPERSEDED for this audit: the SCDA applications page, the SC Code page, the SCDA hemp hub, and the State Plan PDF were all directly opened in this audit and confirm the cited wording. Retain the limitation only as Run 2 history; do not carry it forward as a live caveat on §§7.1–7.2 figures that this audit re-opened. The current State Plan PDF (post-2021) itself remains [VERIFY].

7.3 Hemp Farming Permit (grower) — detail

  • What it allows: as in the table above. A farmer who also processes must hold a Processor Permit as well; a farmer or processor does not need a separate Handler Permit, because those permits already allow handling.
  • Core statutory requirements (§46-55-20): SLED fingerprint state criminal-records check and FBI fingerprint national check, reported to SCDA; SLED may retain fingerprints for certification and for notification of criminal charges; “No person who has been convicted of a felony relating to a controlled substance under state or federal law during a ten-year period from the date of his conviction shall be eligible”; any person who materially falsifies application information is ineligible (§46-55-20(A)(4)).
  • Application requirements evidenced for the 2021 season (flagged as dated — re-confirm for January 2027, do not assume they are unchanged): proof of SC residency; a new background check each permit year; USDA Farm Service Agency (FSA) farm number; GPS coordinates of all growing locations; application and all materials by the deadline; attending an SCDA orientation and signing a Hemp Farming Agreement before possessing any hemp, including clones and seeds; online portal only, no paper applications; a 2020 permit holder would not receive a 2021 permit unless 2020 hemp acreage had been reported to FSA by the deadline.
  • Land requirement (2021 State Plan, via USDA PDF search text): “An applicant may not apply for a permit to grow, cultivate, handle, or process hemp on property that is not owned or leased by that applicant.” Whether the January 2027 application reproduces this wording is [VERIFY].
  • What the farmer permit does not do: it does not authorise processing, does not authorise a retail shop, and does not authorise growing at a location not approved on the application/site-modification request (see Part 11 §11.3).
  • Current status: “Applications for hemp farming are currently closed. The next application will be available in January 2027.” — SCDA applications page, Accessed 2026-10-24. Processor and handler applications are not closed on that page.

7.4 Hemp Processor Permit — detail

  • Issued to individuals only: “SCDA may only issue Processor Permits to individuals. The Applicant Information below is information about the person completing this Application. The Company Information below is information about the processor company.” A business entity alone is not the permittee.
  • Per-location rule: “Each separate address, even if under the same business name, will need its own Processing Permit, Dealer/Handler License, and Weighmaster License.”
  • Pre-conditions: “Anyone processing hemp in the State of South Carolina must successfully complete the full application process with the SCDA and be issued a Hemp Processing Permit prior to processing and prior to taking possession of any in-program harvested hemp materials (biomass) or any other sort of hemp plant material.” “Hemp Processor Permits will be issued once processing facilities have passed inspection.”
  • Sourcing restriction: “Processors may only purchase hemp from South Carolina permit holders or individuals licensed or permitted by another state or Indian tribe.” The same restriction is stated for handlers.
  • Non-compliance consequence (applications page): “Failure to comply with state regulation may result in appropriate action, including suspension from the program and the destruction of hemp materials.”
  • Fee conflict to carry forward, not resolve: a commercial business-plan site lists older figures — Farmer $1,000, Processor $3,000, Handler $1,000 — which are superseded by the live SCDA page and 2024 schedule for processor ($1,500) and handler ($250/$500); the farmer $1,000 figure is the statutory cap / historical figure in the now-resolved $500 vs $1,000 conflict (see Part 2A §4.2 box). Do not quote the $3,000 processor figure as current.

Applicant must be an individual; SCDA does not issue handler permits to business entities. “You cannot cultivate, farm, process, have clones, or possess living (rooted) plant material under this license.” If you hold a Farming or Processor Permit you do not need a Handler Permit.

7.7 Registries — cross-reference only (do not duplicate Run 1 Part 5)

Per Run 1 Part 5, the registries to locate holders are: SCDA “Permitted Hemp Farmers, Handlers, & Processors” plus SCDA sub-lists for Permitted Brokers, Facilities, Labs, R&D, Transporters, and Seedlings/Transplants, all linked from agriculture.sc.gov/hemp/; the USDA plan-review page gives only the State Plan PDF, not a SC licensee list; there is no SCDA retail list, no SLED licence database, and no public SCDOR retail-licence lookup. Run 1's format limitation stands: the SCDA permittee page content was not extractable by text fetch, so whether it is a table, PDF, or searchable database, and whether it has an export button, remains [VERIFY] in a live browser. No current (2025/2026) farmer/handler/processor totals were located in this run either.

7.8 Proposed licences — NOT law, for contrast only

Do not confuse current SCDA permits with the failed/proposed schemes in Run 1 Part 1.9/4.3: S.53 (Compassionate Care Act, medical — 15 cultivation centres, 30 processing facilities, 5 testing labs, 4 transporters, therapeutic cannabis pharmacies, integrated operators) never left Senate Medical Affairs in 2025–2026; S.137's proposed hemp-cannabinoid producer ($500) / retailer ($250 per location) licences (PROPOSED, not H.3924) remain pending; H.3924 failed when the House rejected the conference report 28–69 on 25 June 2026; H.3935's proposed SCDA consumable-hemp licensing and 2% excise died in House Judiciary. None of these creates a current licence type.

9.3 Ballot / referendum history and public opinion polling

9.3.1 Citizen initiatives — NO

South Carolina does NOT allow citizen-initiated statutes or citizen-initiated constitutional amendments. The only route to a statewide ballot question is a legislatively referred constitutional amendment. Primary-law basis, now confirmed from an official legislature source (SC Senate constitution PDF, Article XVI, Section 1, verbatim in substance): an amendment “may be proposed in the Senate or House of Representatives”; “If it is agreed to by two-thirds of the members elected to each House, the amendment or amendments must be entered on the Journals respectively, with the yeas and nays taken on it and must be submitted to the qualified electors of the State at the next general election for Representatives”; “If a majority of the electors qualified to vote for members of the General Assembly voting on the question vote in favor of the amendment or amendments and a majority of each branch of the next General Assembly, after the election and before another, ratify the amendment or amendments, by yeas and nays, they become part of the Constitution”; and the amendment “must be read three times, on three several days, in each House.” Do not omit the ratification step — voter approval alone does not enact an SC constitutional amendment. Article XVI, Section 3 separately allows a constitutional convention on a two-thirds vote of each branch plus a voter vote.

Traps to avoid: S.39, Session 124 (2021–2022), “S.C. Constitutional amendments, initiative petition and referendum,” would have created an initiative-petition/referendum process (signatures including ≥2% from each of at least two-thirds of counties, submission to the State Election Commission by 1 June of an odd-numbered year, 60-day certification, one 30-day supplemental-petition period). S.39 did NOT become law — its text on scstatehouse.gov is a proposed bill, not current constitutional law. A third-party site (stateregstoday.com) incorrectly states SC initiatives can amend the constitution via Article XVI signature collection — do not use it; flag it as erroneous if mentioned.

No statewide binding cannabis ballot measure was found. No legislatively referred constitutional amendment on cannabis, and no citizen initiative on cannabis (impossible — see above), has been placed on a statewide general-election ballot as far as scstatehouse.gov / SC Votes / Ballotpedia searches establish. Phrase as “none located … as accessed 24 October 2026” unless a full Ballotpedia SC ballot-measure list is opened and checked.

9.3.2 Advisory primary ballot question — YES, one verified, Democratic primary only, non-binding

12 June 2018 Democratic primary — advisory question, legal effect: none.

  • Question (verbatim, SCETV 2018 primary results, 13 June 2018, and Marijuana Moment): “Do you support passing a state law allowing doctors to prescribe medical marijuana to patients?”
  • Result: Yes 82.03%, No 17.97% (SCETV, “2018 Primary Results,” under “ADVISORY QUESTIONS — Democratic Question 1”). Marijuana Moment (published 13 June 2018, updated 17 June 2018) rounds this as “approved by an 82% to 18% margin”; an election-night partial count (>93% of precincts) was 81% / 19% — the 82.03/17.97 figure is the fuller compilation and supersedes the partial count; explain the difference if both are mentioned.
  • Who voted: Democratic primary voters only. Former U.S. Attorney Bill Nettles reportedly pushed both parties to place the question on their primary ballots; only Democrats agreed (Marijuana Moment). SC has open primaries, so a voter could choose either party's ballot — not everyone voting on the Democratic question was necessarily a Democrat.
  • Context from the same article: House and Senate committees had approved medical cannabis legislation that year, but the bills never advanced to floor votes in either chamber that year; several thousand more people voted on the medical cannabis measure than selected a candidate in the Democratic gubernatorial primary on the same ballot.
  • Raw Yes/No vote totals for the 2018 advisory question: [UNAVAILABLE] in the text retrieved — not located from SC Votes (scvotes.gov / enr-scvotes.org) in this research. Do not invent totals from the percentages.

Yes / No.” History: Senate introduced/read first time 19 Jan 2022, referred to Committee on Judiciary, no passage shown. This referendum was NOT held. Do not report a 2022 statewide advisory result.

10.2 Interstate: hemp shipments, products bought legally elsewhere, NC/GA conflicts, agreements

10.2.1 Federal interstate hemp protection — and its limits

  • Statutory note to 7 USC §1639o (2018 Farm Bill, Pub. L. 115-334, Title X, §10114, 20 Dec 2018, 132 Stat. 4914), from search-result text of US Code / USDA legal opinion summaries: (a) Rule of Construction: “Nothing in this title … prohibits the interstate commerce of hemp (as defined in section 297A of the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946 [7 U.S.C. 1639o]) or hemp products.” (b) Transportation of Hemp and Hemp Products: “No State or Indian Tribe shall prohibit the transportation or shipment of hemp or hemp products produced in accordance with subtitle G of the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946 [7 U.S.C. 1639o et seq.] through the State or the territory of the Indian Tribe, as applicable.”
  • USDA legal opinion summary (JD Supra / Beveridge & Diamond, June 2019, via search): After USDA publishes regulations implementing 2018 Farm Bill hemp provisions, states/tribes may not prohibit interstate transportation/shipment of hemp lawfully produced under a State or Tribal plan or under a USDA plan; §10114 preempts state law to the extent it prohibits interstate transportation/shipment of hemp produced in accordance with AMA subtitle G. Secondary legal-clarity summaries add a practical warning: protection is for lawfully produced hemp only, does not prevent roadside stops/seizure where an officer cannot distinguish hemp from marijuana by sight/smell, and documentation (licence, manifest, COA) is the practical safeguard — secondary, not a statute, label as such.
  • Critical limit for South Carolina — analytical, label as such: Federal protection covers hemp “produced in accordance with subtitle G” and, in the current federal definition, hemp as defined federally. It does NOT make a product lawful in South Carolina if, under SC law as enforced, it is marijuana (e.g. >0.3% delta-9, or a delta-8/isomer product treated as Schedule I under the AG/SLED position). The through-shipment vs destination-sale distinction matters: §10114(b) speaks to transportation/shipment “through” the State; it does not create a right to sell a non-compliant product at destination in SC.

10.2.2 South Carolina hemp shipment law — current law

  • §46-55-30 (Run 1, verbatim): “The provisions contained in this chapter do not apply to the possession, handling, transport, or sale of hemp products and extracts, including those containing hemp-derived cannabinoids, including CBD. Nothing in this chapter authorizes any person to violate any federal or state law or regulation.” Run 1 treats this as the reason SC has no state hemp-retail licence, packaging, labelling or buffer regime in Chapter 55.
  • No SC statute creating a hemp-transport permit, manifest, or COA-carry requirement for hemp products was located in this session [UNAVAILABLE/VERIFY — SCDA State Plan transport provisions not opened].
  • Do not conflate: SCDA Handler Permit categories in Run 1 include Transporter ($100 application + $250 permit fee per 2024 schedule, $10 per driver Transporter ID card on the 2023 form). That is a handler permit for handling/transporting hemp plant material under the State Plan, NOT a general hemp-product shipment licence.

10.2.3 Proposed through-transport and direct-shipment provisions — PROPOSED only, NOT law

From search-result text of H.3924 amended text (LegiScan, 2025) and Run 1 §1.9 — all from failed/proposed bill versions, NOT current SC law. The final H.3924 conference text and the H.4758/H.4759 texts must be checked before attributing any of these provisions to a specific bill version:

  • Proposed §46-55-80 (in H.3924/H.4758-type drafts): “Nothing in this chapter may be construed to prohibit the continuous transportation through South Carolina of the plant Cannabis sativa L., and any part of that plant, including the seeds thereof and all derivatives, extracts, cannabinoids, isomers, acids, salts, and salts of isomers, whether growing or not, with a delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol concentration of not more than three-tenths percent (0.3%) on a dry weight basis, produced in accordance with 7 U.S.C Section 1639 et. seq.”
  • Proposed §46-55-70 (in same drafts): intoxicating hemp product or hemp product containing higher total THC than specified in §46-55-10(4) distributed/sold/offered for sale in violation of the chapter shall be considered contraband and may be seized; sale/possession of such product prohibited and punishable in same manner as THC under §§44-53-190 and 44-53-370; unlawful to manufacture/distribute/sell/offer for sale/possess with intent to distribute any beverage exceeding total THC limit.
  • Proposed §46-55-70(D) (in same drafts): “Online sales, direct delivery, and direct shipments of consumable hemp products within or into this State are strictly prohibited. For purposes of this section, 'direct shipment' means the shipment of any consumable hemp product from any producer or retailer of consumable hemp products directly to a resident of this State. A person who violates this subsection is guilty of a misdemeanor and, upon conviction, must be fined not more than three thousand dollars or imprisoned for three years, or both.”
  • Proposed §46-55-90 (in same drafts): “Nothing in this chapter may be construed to prohibit the possession, manufacture, sale, or distribution of CBD products, provided those products do not produce an intoxicating or psychoactive reaction when consumed by a person.”

10.2.4 Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians (EBCI), North Carolina — products bought legally elsewhere and SC law on bringing them in

  • EBCI is a federally recognised tribe in North Carolina, NOT in South Carolina. SCDAH's consultation list includes EBCI as a historically affiliated tribe, not a SC-resident tribe.
  • EBCI framework (secondary sources in this session, consistent with NC Run 1 — re-check the NC Run 1 file if NC pinpoints are wanted, do not copy NC Run 1 memory figures as new SC research): Medical cannabis legalised by EBCI in 2021, medical Ord. No. 539 (2021); adult-use referendum 7 Sept 2023 passed 2,464–1,057; adult-use Ord. No. 63 approved 27 June 2024 (One Feather search result: “Ord. No. 63 (2024), authorizing adult-use cannabis on the lands of the EBCI was approved as amended on June 27, 2024 and signed into law by Principal Chief Michell Hicks the same day”); Great Smoky Cannabis Company, operated by Qualla Enterprises, LLC (tribal entity), began medical sales 20 Apr 2024 and adult-use sales to all adults 21+ on 7 Sept 2024; tribal Cannabis Control Board handles licensing/compliance; seed-to-sale tracking, testing for potency/pesticides/heavy metals/microbial contaminants (secondary). Qualla Boundary: roughly 57,000-acre tribal land trust in western NC, about an hour east of Asheville, three miles from Oconaluftee Visitor Center of Great Smoky Mountains National Park (secondary). On-Boundary only rule — secondary consensus: “Cannabis becomes illegal the moment it crosses the Boundary line”; “All cannabis must be consumed on the Qualla Boundary. Leaving the Boundary triggers NC state law immediately”; “products purchased at Great Smoky Cannabis Co. cannot legally be taken off tribal land” (secondary). One Feather 25 Aug 2026 article notes first adult-use purchaser on 7 Sept 2024 was Ben Cordell of Greenville, SC, first in line — that anecdote does NOT make transport to SC lawful.
  • EBCI operation scale — secondary only, NOT official EBCI figures: MMJ Daily article (mid-Oct 2026) and Cardinal Pine article (Oct 2026): operation spans seed-to-sale, facilities can hold up to 150,000 plants, production nearing 80,000 pounds in 2026 and expected to exceed 110,000 pounds in 2027, over 3.5 million products sold, approaching 1 million customer visits, about 270 employees, over 85% enrolled tribal members, production cost per gram fell 50% in past year, tribal sales tax revenue topped $5 million in 2026, tribal tax rate 9% in Cardinal Pine calculation (implying >$55.6 million product over roughly nine months). The NC Run 1 tribal tax conflict (7.5% vs 9%) remains unresolved. Do not quote scale/tax figures as official in Part 10.
  • EBCI hemp stores — PROPOSED ordinance only: Cherokee One Feather, 22 Oct 2026, “Ordinances submitted during Annual Council deal with bear hunting, hemp stores, and more” — proposed amendment to Cherokee Code Section 17A-4 (Hemp store license) stating multiple businesses on EBCI trust lands sell hemp/hemp products, some owned/operated by enrolled members, some by non-members, several businesses selling CBD products have violated tribal law, e.g. selling to minors, selling prohibited intoxicating hemp products, violating EBCI Cannabis Control Board regulations; majority of violations at non-member-owned/operated businesses; proposal: “Hemp store licenses may only be issued to enrolled members, businesses wholly-owned by the enrolled members, or businesses wholly-owned by the Tribe.” This is a submitted/proposed ordinance as of 22 Oct 2026, NOT an enacted EBCI law in the retrieved text.
  • SC law on bringing EBCI cannabis into SC — by application of Run 1 statutes (analytical application, not a located SC-EBCI ruling): EBCI tribal permission does not travel. Once the product is in SC, SC law applies: marijuana as defined in §44-53-110(27) is Schedule I (§44-53-190(D)); possession is charged under §44-53-370(d)(5) (≤1 oz misdemeanor, Run 1) or (d)(2)/(a)/(b)/(e) for larger amounts, distribution, or trafficking, subject to Julian's Law exclusions only (≤0.9% THC, >15% CBD, written SC physician certification for severe epilepsy, or FDA-approved clinical-trial product). An EBCI adult-use purchase (21+, tribal tax paid, tribal packaging) does NOT satisfy Julian's Law, does NOT create SC reciprocity (Run 1: no out-of-state reciprocity in statute [VERIFY]), and does NOT create a SC medical licence. A product that is hemp under EBCI/NC law but is >0.3% delta-9, or is a delta-8/isomer product treated as Schedule I under the AG's advisory opinion (not law) and SLED's enforcement position; no SC appellate court holding construing the Hemp Farming Act on delta-8/THCA was located, is likewise at risk in SC even if it was lawfully bought on the Qualla Boundary as hemp. No SC “safe harbour,” “transport through,” or “personal import” exception for EBCI cannabis was located [UNAVAILABLE]. The federal interstate hemp protection in 7 USC §1639o note does NOT apply to marijuana (cannabis above the federal hemp definition), and EBCI adult-use cannabis is marijuana under federal law as well as SC law, subject to the split-scheduling baseline (adult-use remains Schedule I federally). Practical enforcement note — secondary only: NC senators' letter (Sens. Thom Tillis and Ted Budd, Mar 2024) asked federal/state/local officials what steps they were taking to enforce marijuana prohibition in light of EBCI sales; Rep. Chuck Edwards (NC) opposed EBCI legalisation in a Cherokee One Feather op-ed ahead of the adult-use vote. Those are political statements, NOT SC enforcement policy. No SC AG/SLED statement specifically on EBCI purchases transported to SC was located [UNAVAILABLE].

10.2.5 North Carolina conflict — summary

  • NC statewide: No adult-use or comprehensive medical programme; small possession remains a misdemeanor; narrow epilepsy-extract provision remains; personal cultivation no allowance under state law (secondary summary, consistent with NC Run 1). Under NC General Statutes §90-95, criminal consequences depend on quantity/conduct, misdemeanors for simple possession of less than 1.5 ounces, felony for larger amounts/resin extracts, trafficking mandatory minimums for more than ten pounds (secondary).
  • NC hemp (secondary-supported, with statute pinpoints): Delta-9 THC in hemp must not exceed 0.3% dry weight (G.S. 90-87); hemp and hemp products ≤0.3% Δ9-THC are excluded from the Controlled Substances Act (S.L. 2022-32, effective 30 June 2022); no state-level age restriction yet — proposed bills would set minimum age at 21; hemp cultivation regulated federally via USDA; NC no longer issues grower/processor licenses.
  • NC hemp bills — NOT law: HB 328 (NC) — Senate adopted conference report 37–6 on 2 July 2026, sits in House Rules re-referred 30 July 2026, no final House vote per NC Run 1; a late Aug 2026 law-firm summary states it “sits one House vote away from becoming law.” Those two statements are consistent (conference report awaiting House action), not contradictory. HB 328 would create a regulated market for hemp-derived consumable products with 21+ sales restrictions, licensing, and criminal penalties. HB 607 and SB 328 pending, SB 265 dead, SB 711 Senate-passed 2022/House-killed, per NC Run 1 — do not import NC bills into SC Part 10.
  • Conflict in practice: NC and SC share the delta-9 ≤0.3% hemp test, so a plain delta-9-compliant hemp product is on the same definitional footing in both states, BUT SC's AG/SLED isomer position (delta-8 and other isomers not legalised in themselves) and SC's contested smokable-flower position create a SC enforcement risk that does not automatically follow from NC hemp status. Conversely, NC's EBCI tribal cannabis permission has no counterpart in SC and no SC recognition.

10.2.6 Georgia conflict — summary (ALL Georgia details below are secondary unless stated; [VERIFY against O.C.G.A. and Georgia Department of Agriculture rules before presenting as settled GA law])

  • GA hemp framework (secondary consensus): Georgia Department of Agriculture administers the hemp programme, licensing for growers/processors and, for consumable hemp, retailers/wholesalers/manufacturers; testing laboratories must satisfy registration/accreditation; every product needs a current certificate of analysis.
  • GA measurement — the opposite of SC's current test: Total THC, not delta-9 only — Total THC = measured delta-9 THC + 87.7% of THCA, per O.C.G.A. §2-23-3.1 and SB 494 (secondary). Any finished product whose calculated total THC exceeds 0.3% dry weight is legally marijuana, Schedule I under GA state law (secondary). Two-way trap: A SC delta-9-compliant THCA flower product can fail GA total-THC, and a GA total-THC-compliant processed product can still fail SC's isomer position if it contains delta-8/HHC etc. treated as Schedule I in SC.
  • GA product rules (secondary): Unprocessed hemp flower/leaves retail sale banned regardless of THC content (GA Rules 40-32-5, via secondary); hemp-infused “food products” such as cookies, brownies, candy prohibited, with gummies and beverages as deliberate exceptions; gummies capped at 10 mg total delta-9 THC each and 300 mg per package; beverages capped at 10 mg per 12 fluid ounces, proportionately less for smaller drinks, containers no larger than 12 ounces; tinctures no more than 2 mg per millilitre in containers up to 60 millilitres; topicals 1,000 mg package limit; packaging must carry state THC warning symbol and be child-resistant, with COA QR code (secondary); consumable hemp buyers must be 21 or older; retailers must hold a Retail Consumable Hemp Establishment License; retail locations must post age-restriction signage and be >500 ft from K-12 schools (secondary).
  • GA delta-8/delta-10 — secondary conflict, do not resolve: One secondary states delta-8/delta-10 remain on GA shelves for now under the same total-THC and licensing rules; another secondary states GA law does not explicitly address delta-8/delta-10/HHC by name — status unknown. Carry the conflict.
  • GA marijuana penalties (secondary only): If a delta-8 product exceeds 0.3% delta-9 THC, it no longer qualifies as hemp, becomes marijuana, and possession faces GA marijuana penalties; GA treats marijuana possession as a felony under O.C.G.A. §16-13-30, conviction 1–10 years, possession of 1 oz or less generally treated as misdemeanor, more than 1 oz triggers the full felony range, some local decriminalisation — [VERIFY against O.C.G.A. before use].
  • GA vs SC practical conflict: A product lawful to sell in GA only with a GA licence, total-THC COA, age-21 sale, and school buffer cannot be assumed lawful in SC, where there is no retail licence, no age rule, no total-THC test, and no COA requirement in current law, but where SC isomer enforcement may treat the same product as marijuana. Conversely, a SC shop selling an unlicensed, untested delta-8 product to a person under 21 would violate GA rules if that sale occurred in GA, but SC current law has no equivalent retail rule — that absence is NOT a GA defence.

PART 11: OPERATIONS RULES

Framing rule for the whole of Part 11: Chapter 55 regulates cultivation, handling, and processing of hemp. By §46-55-30 it “do[es] not apply to the possession, handling, transport, or sale of hemp products and extracts, including those containing hemp-derived cannabinoids, including CBD.” That single sentence is why most retail-facing operations rules below are “no SC hemp-specific rule” — a finished CBD/hemp retail shop is outside Chapter 55 and is governed only by general law (food, consumer protection, tax registration, local zoning/business licence — Run 1 Parts 1.6, 2, 3). Do not import the failed bills' testing, labelling, age, or advertising rules into current law.

11.1 Testing — required tests, sampling, failed tests and recalls, labs

What is tested, and when — cultivation compliance testing only: SCDA's 2020 approval release: the State Plan “mandates that SCDA staff sample every hemp field in the state prior to harvest.” SCDA Fee & Reporting Schedule (2024): “Sample Request — This report is due 15 days prior to anticipated sample collection date. Once official sample is collected, plants must be harvested within 30 days.” The 2026 Sample Request Form states the same lead time in different words: “This report is due 15 days prior to anticipated sample collection date. Following the submission of this form, a SCDA inspector will schedule an appointment to collect sample(s).” “No harvest or destruction is authorized until you receive approval in writing from SCDA.” “SCDA Inspector(s) may only take samples from the Growing Sites set forth on this Sample Request Form” and will not sample additional locations not on the form. “The SCDA Hemp Farming Program will not complete sample preparation as part of the sample collection process. Samples will be placed in a non-air tight paper bag to encourage air flow, but the SCDA Hemp Farming Program will not dry, cure, ground, mill, or otherwise prepare the sample.” HempFeeReportingSchedule2024.pdf; SCHempSampleRequestForm2026.pdf. Accessed 2026-10-24.

Distinguish three different “15/30 day” figures — do not conflate them: (a) SCDA sample-request lead time = 15 days before anticipated sample collection; (b) SCDA harvest deadline after official sampling = within 30 days; (c) the original USDA interim rule's sampling window = within 15 days before anticipated harvest, expanded by the USDA final rule to 30 days. The SCDA documents retrieved here use (a) + (b); whether SC's current plan text adopts the federal 30-day collection window verbatim is [VERIFY] against the current plan.

Method (federal/state-plan level): post-decarboxylation or similarly reliable methods; gas or liquid chromatography with detection are the methodologies named in USDA rule summaries; total THC is determined and reported on a dry-weight basis, accounting for conversion of THCA into THC. SCDA's own 2019 interim-rule summary states the same: samples “MUST be tested using postdecarboxylation or other similarly reliable analytical methods where the total THC concentration level reported accounts for the conversion of [THCA] into THC,” and “Samples must be delivered to a DEA registered laboratory for testing.”

Measurement-of-uncertainty / “acceptable hemp THC level”: under the USDA framework, a sample is hemp if 0.3% falls within the laboratory's measurement-of-uncertainty distribution (e.g. a 0.35% result with ±0.06% uncertainty spans 0.29–0.41% and counts as hemp). SCDA's current applications-page text phrases this as total THC “at or below 0.3 percent (after accounting for the measurement of uncertainty, which is likely less than a 0.099% variance) or be subject to destruction.” That 0.099% figure is SCDA applications-page text retrieved by search, not a figure in Chapter 55 — [VERIFY] in a live browser before quoting it as a rule.

THC-formula conflict — flagged, not resolved (resolve before publication): Run 1 / Chapter 55 text: hemp = “a delta-9 THC concentration of not more than 0.3 percent on a dry weight basis” (§46-55-10(6)). SCDA applications page (search text, undated in fetch): “Federal law now requires that all states have a testing protocol to measure delta-9 THC post-decarboxylation – this means total THC must be not more than 0.3 percent,” and for processors: “‘hemp’ means … with a total THC concentration of not more than 0.3 percent on a dry weight basis. This Processing Permit does not give you the ability to process or possess materials with a total THC concentration of more than 0.3 percent.” USDA State Plan / federal rule: total THC (THC + THCA, post-decarboxylation) is the compliance measure for licensed production. Do not publish a single sentence saying “SC law is total-THC” or “SC law is delta-9-based” without resolving this. The accurate interim formulation is: the statute as printed in Run 1 is delta-9-based; the SCDA programme material and the USDA-approved plan apply a post-decarboxylation total-THC compliance test to licensed production. The same tension applies to the post-11 December 2026 federal definition (PL 119-37/119-103), on which Run 1 found no SC official response [UNAVAILABLE].

Failed tests, remediation, and destruction — version conflict, flagged: 2021 State Plan (USDA PDF, search text): a lot represented by a sample above the federally defined THC level “shall be disposed of in accordance with the on-farm disposal options described herein and prohibited from being further handled, processed, or entering the stream of commerce.” Farmers must submit and have SCDA approve a destruction plan prior to destruction. Farmers notified of an over-limit lot “must arrange for either disposal or remediation.” Remediation = “disposing of flower materials and salvaging the remainder of the plant or blending the entire plant into biomass plant material”; post-remediation re-sampling/testing must occur, and only crops testing at or below the level may enter commerce; all remaining noncompliant crops must then be disposed. “No destruction may occur unless Department personnel are present to witness the destruction unless otherwise set forth by an exception in writing by the Department.” Farmers must document disposal/remediation (copy to USDA). SCDA current applications page (search text): “Federal law will no longer allow SC to have a remediation safeguard. Now hemp total THC must test at or below 0.3 percent (after accounting for the measurement of uncertainty …) or be subject to destruction.” These two statements cannot both describe the current plan. Either the plan was amended after the 2021 version retrieved here, or the applications page overstates the federal position. Parent action: pull the current State Plan version from the USDA plan-review page and confirm whether remediation survives; do not quote the 2021 remediation procedure as current law until then.

Negligent-violation threshold — also in conflict: SCDA applications page: “cultivating, handling, or processing hemp with a total THC level greater than 0.5% will constitute a ‘negligent violation’.” Run 1 / §46-55-40: a negligent violation includes producing Cannabis sativa L. above the federally defined THC level, with a corrective action plan as the sole remedy and five-year ineligibility after three negligent violations in five years. Secondary summaries of the USDA final rule put the federal negligence threshold at 1.0% total THC (0.3–1.0% = remediation/disposal but not negligent; above 1.0% = negligent). Do not quote 0.5% or 1.0% as the SC threshold without checking which document SCDA currently enforces. What is consistent across all three sources: a culpable-mental-state-greater-than-negligence violation must be reported to the AG and SLED Chief (§46-55-40, Run 1), and three negligent violations in five years = five-year suspension/ineligibility (applications page: “If a Permitted [Handler/Processor] has three negligent violations in 5 years, he or she will face permit suspension for five years”).

SCDA sample pricing (not a lab market price): Inspector visit $10; non-SCDA-issued PPE visit $25; per-sample $10; resample $15; farmer pays shipping (2024 Fee Schedule). A secondary site's claim that farmers bear $250–$300 per sample for laboratory analysis was not corroborated on an SCDA page and must not be quoted as an SCDA price.

Recalls — finished products: No SC hemp-specific recall procedure for finished hemp/CBD retail products was located, because Chapter 55 excludes sale of hemp products (§46-55-30). There is no SC hemp-product recall register, recall-notice rule, or retail-product failed-test procedure in the material retrieved. General food/consumer-protection law may apply [VERIFY — no SCDA/DPH hemp-product recall guidance was opened]. Do not import the failed bills' testing/recall panels (cannabinoids, heavy metals, pesticides) as current law.

Retesting: the secondary claim “Retesting is not permitted” was not corroborated on an SCDA page in this run; the 2024 schedule does price a “resample” at $15, which cuts against a blanket no-retest claim. [VERIFY — resample vs retest distinction on the current SCDA forms.]

Certified / accredited labs serving SC, including DEA-registered labs: No named list of SC DEA-registered laboratories was located in this run. The closest official roster is SCDA's “Permitted Labs” list (Run 1 Part 5), whose contents/format were not extractable by text fetch — cross-reference only, do not invent names. What a SCDA lab handler must show (2023 Handler Application): copy of DEA registration, copy of test standards and methods, copy of ISO 17025 accreditation or, if not ISO-accredited, copy of other accreditation(s). That is a permit-application requirement for a handler laboratory, not a published SC lab directory. DEA-registration enforcement delay (federal, from Run 1 baseline and corroborated by secondary USDA summaries): USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026; during the delay, compliance testing may be performed by non-DEA-registered laboratories provided the laboratory and arrangement otherwise satisfy the applicable hemp programme. The delay is enforcement discretion, not repeal, and does not suspend sampling, THC testing, reporting, licensing, or disposal rules. No SC-specific list of ISO-certified labs, and no SC requirement for a particular contaminant panel (pesticides, heavy metals, solvents, microbials) for finished products, was located [UNAVAILABLE for finished products; for crop compliance, the only required test evidenced is THC concentration].

11.2 Licence rules — transfers, ownership, renewals, relocation, revocation, insurance/bonding

  • Transfers of the permit itself: No SC hemp-permit transfer rule was located in Chapter 55 or in the SCDA application material retrieved. Do not state that a permit is transferable.   • Ownership changes: No express ownership-change rule located. Because processor and handler permits are issued to individuals (not business entities), a change of the individual permittee cannot be assumed to be a mere notification; the conservative, flagged formulation is: change of permittee [VERIFY — treat as requiring a new application unless SCDA confirms otherwise]. A change of the underlying company name/address where the same individual remains permittee is likewise [VERIFY].

For processors/handlers, each separate address needs its own permit/licences (see §7.4) — a move to a new address is therefore a new per-location permit, not a relocation of the old one, on the evidence retrieved. [VERIFY the processor/handler site-change form, if any, before stating a single relocation procedure.]

Three negligent violations in five years = five-year suspension/ineligibility. Material falsification = ineligibility (§46-55-20(A)(4)). Harvesting before SCDA sampling, or failing to submit a Harvest/Destruction Report on time, “may be subject to crop destruction and regulatory action up to and including permit suspension or revocation” (2021 State Plan, search text). No separate hemp-permit bond amount was located. Do not confuse the mining bond in §48-20-110 or any other Title 48/58 bond found in search with a hemp requirement.

11.3 Cultivation rules — plot registration, background checks, sampling before harvest, indoor/outdoor

  • Plot registration (legal description + GPS + FSA): §46-55-20(B)(1) requires land legal description and GPS coordinates (Run 1 §1.7). USDA-plan level: SCDA must collect and maintain for at least three years information on hemp production sites, including legal description and geospatial location; licensed producers must report hemp crop acreage to USDA FSA. 2021 farmer requirements add the FSA farm number and GPS coordinates of all locations (see §7.3). §46-55-20(A)(5): licensee/land information must be accessible in real time to federal, state, and local law enforcement.
  • Background checks: SLED + FBI fingerprint checks; 10-year controlled-substance felony bar; material falsification = ineligibility (see §7.3). A new check was required each permit year in 2021 — current-cycle rule [VERIFY for 2027].
  • Sampling before harvest: see §11.1 in full — SCDA inspector collects the official sample from growing sites on the Sample Request Form only; no harvest or destruction until SCDA written approval; harvest within 30 days of official sampling; harvest report within 72 hours of completing harvest for each growing location (2024 Fee Schedule).
  • Indoor vs outdoor: Both are covered, with different reporting cadences in the 2021 State Plan / 2024 schedule: Field (outdoor): planting report due 15 days after planting; if a growing location on record is not planted by July 31, submit a “no plant” report. Greenhouse / indoor: planting report due 15 days after planting, and quarterly thereafter: March 31 / June 30 / September 30 / December 31. The 2021 plan phrases the greenhouse rule as a completed planting report for each greenhouse/indoor structure by those four dates each year after initial planting. Destruction forms likewise cover “every field or indoor area planted.” No indoor-specific lighting, HVAC, or canopy rule, and no outdoor setback/fencing rule, was located in the hemp material retrieved. The secondary “No direct fencing is required” line comes from the outdated pilot-era page and must not be presented as a current rule without an SCDA source. [VERIFY indoor/outdoor operating rules on the current forms.]
  • Other cultivation duties evidenced (2021 State Plan): monitor and destroy volunteer hemp plants from the permittee's cultivation for three years after cultivation ends; submit Harvest/Destruction reports prior to intended harvest or destruction of a failed crop; do not store/cultivate live plants at unapproved locations; acreage/site changes only via the $50 amendment process (see §11.2).

12.1 Paraphernalia and smoke/vape shop rules

12.1.1 State paraphernalia law — §44-53-391 (Run 1 [VERIFY] now partially upgraded)

Text opened in this session via Justia 2022 Code reproduction: §44-53-391, Justia 2022. Accessed 2026-10-24.

  • (a) “It shall be unlawful for any person to advertise for sale, manufacture, possess, sell or deliver, or to possess with the intent to deliver, or sell paraphernalia.”
  • (b) In determining whether an object is paraphernalia, a court or other authority shall consider, in addition to all other logically relevant factors: (1) statements by owner/person in control concerning use; (2) proximity to controlled substances; (3) existence of residue; (4) direct/circumstantial evidence of intent to deliver to persons whom owner knows or should reasonably know intend to use object to facilitate violation of law (innocence as to direct violation does not prevent finding of intended/designed use); (5) instructions, oral/written, provided with object; (6) descriptive materials accompanying object explaining/depicting use; (7) national/local advertising concerning use; (8) manner displayed for sale; (9) whether owner/person in control is legitimate supplier of like/related items, e.g. licensed distributor/dealer of tobacco products; (10) direct/circumstantial evidence of ratio of sales of object to total sales of business; (11) existence/scope of legitimate uses in community; (12) expert testimony.
  • (c) “Any person found guilty of violating the provisions of this section shall be subject to a civil fine of not more than five hundred dollars except that a corporation shall be subject to a civil fine of not more than fifty thousand dollars. Imposition of such fine shall not give rise to any disability or legal disadvantage based on conviction for a criminal offense.”
  • History: 1982 Act No. 400, Section 2.

Status upgrade, stated precisely: This Justia 2022 opening confirms the Run 1 secondary text for §44-53-391. Upgrade Run 1's [VERIFY] to “text confirmed in Justia 2022 reproduction, current scstatehouse.gov version still to be checked” — do not claim a scstatehouse.gov opening for §44-53-391.

Definition scope (Run 1 §1.2): §44-53-110(33) “Paraphernalia” includes marijuana/hashish pipes, water pipes, bongs, roach clips, etc., but “does not include cigarette papers and tobacco pipes.” That definition and §44-53-391 must be read together; a dual-use item's status turns on the §44-53-391(b) factors, especially statements, residue, proximity, display, and advertising.

AG opinion, 25 July 1996, Hon. Dennis E. Phipps (scag.gov PDF, via search): “Section 44-53-391 does not make the acts forbidden therein subject to criminal penalties. Instead, the Act speaks of the imposition of a 'civil fine' for violation thereof… 'shall not give rise to any disability or legal disadvantage based on conviction for a criminal offense.'” Opinion, not law, but consistent with the statute text. AG opinion, 25 July 1996 (PDF). Accessed 2026-10-24.

Practical consequence — secondary law-firm consensus, label as secondary: paraphernalia alone under state law is a civil ticket, not a misdemeanor/felony, with no jail sentence under state law; it commonly accompanies a possession charge, which is a criminal drug charge, and admitting an item was used as paraphernalia can open the door to more severe drug charges. Do not present that practical warning as a statute.

Municipal exception — secondary only, [VERIFY in Columbia code]: Touma Law Group (Columbia, via search, updated 12 days before search) states: inside Columbia, City Council adopted an ordinance in Aug 2023 making it unlawful to use, or possess with intent to use, paraphernalia within the city, Section 14-355 sets penalty at fine up to $500 or up to 30 days in jail, charge goes through Columbia Municipal Court, state citation is civil while city charge carries jail exposure. Kent Collins Law Firm secondary summaries agree in general: each city can have its own ordinance punishable as misdemeanor, up to 30 days in jail. Do NOT present the Columbia §14-355 ordinance as verified law without opening the current Columbia Code; present it as secondary-reported municipal variation that is the key exception to the “state paraphernalia is civil only” headline. Touma Law Group, possession of drug paraphernalia (secondary). Accessed 2026-10-24.

Do not merge Columbia's two ordinances: Ord. 2022-082 warning-sign rule (Run 1, first reading only, final adoption [VERIFY]) is a seller signage rule — warning signs equal to 50% of size of signs selling the product, warning product may cause failed workplace drug test — NOT a paraphernalia criminal ordinance. The Aug 2023 §14-355 paraphernalia ordinance (secondary, above) is separate.

  • Other tobacco/vaping rules — secondary only: All nicotine liquid sold in SC must be packaged in child-resistant containers meeting CPSC testing standards, 15 USC §1472a (federal); vending machines selling e-cigarettes restricted to locations inaccessible to minors such as bars/private clubs (secondary); operators must keep updated list of every machine's location on file with Department (DOR Other Tobacco Products, secondary). Label as secondary/federal, not SC hemp rules.

12.1.4 New 2026 ENDS directory law — VERIFIED ENACTED (this resolves a prior open question)

Official bill page opened in this session: 2025-2026 Bill 287, Electronic Nicotine Delivery System Regulation, S.287 bill page. Accessed 2026-10-24.

  • Status — enacted: “A97, R101, S287”; Introduced Senate 29 Jan 2025; Introduced House 25 Mar 2025; Last Amended 21 Jan 2026; Governor's Action: 27 Feb 2026, Signed; Effective date 27 Feb 2026; Act No. 97; Ratified R 101 on 25 Feb 2026; page last updated 15 Apr 2026.
  • What it enacts: “AN ACT TO AMEND THE SOUTH CAROLINA CODE OF LAWS BY ADDING SECTION 44-95-65 SO AS TO PROVIDE REGULATIONS FOR THE SALE OF ELECTRONIC NICOTINE DELIVERY SYSTEMS, TO PROVIDE PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS OF THE SECTION, AND TO PROVIDE CERTAIN TIMELINES AND EFFECTIVE DATES; AND BY AMENDING SECTION 16-17-501, RELATING TO TERMS DEFINED IN THE 'YOUTH ACCESS TO TOBACCO PREVENTION ACT,' SO AS TO CHANGE THE DEFINITION OF 'ELECTRONIC SMOKING DEVICE'.”
  • §44-95-65(A)(3) “ENDS product” — nicotine-only definition (verbatim in substance): “an electronic nicotine delivery system intended for eventual retail sale in this State that is a noncombustible product that employs a heating element, power source, electronic circuit, or other electronic, chemical, or mechanical means, regardless of shape or size to produce vapor from nicotine in a solution. ENDS product includes a consumable nicotine liquid solution suitable for use in an electronic nicotine delivery system, whether sold with the ENDS product or separately, but does not include any product regulated as a drug or device under Chapter V of the federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.” Scope limit — [VERIFY]: Whether the ENDS directory covers THC/hemp vapes, nicotine-free vapes, or CBD vapes is NOT resolved by this definition on its face (it says nicotine in a solution); do not assume THC vapes are in or out of the directory.
  • Manufacturer certification — §44-95-65(B)–(D): Every manufacturer of ENDS products sold in SC, directly or through distributor/retailer/intermediary, shall annually execute and deliver under penalty of perjury to the Attorney General a certification verifying either: (1) the ENDS product was on the market in the US as of 8 Aug 2016 and the manufacturer applied for a marketing order under 21 U.S.C. §387j by submitting a premarket tobacco product application on or before 9 Sept 2020, and the application remains under review or a marketing denial order has been stayed/rescinded/vacated; or (2) the manufacturer has received a marketing granted order under 21 U.S.C. §387j. Certification must separately list brand name, category, product name, flavour, and foreign manufacturer name/address for each product.
  • AG directory — §44-95-65(G)–(H): AG shall develop and maintain a directory listing all manufacturers that have provided certifications and all ENDS products listed in those certifications; make it available for public inspection on its website; update monthly; send monthly notifications to registered wholesalers/retailers/manufacturers or make changes prominent on the AG website.
  • Fees — §44-95-65(J) (this resolves the earlier $2,000/$500 vs $50 conflict in favour of the enacted text): “A nonrefundable fee of one hundred dollars for each ENDS product shall be paid the first time a manufacturer submits a certification form… The Attorney General shall thereafter collect an annual renewal fee of fifty dollars for each ENDS product.” Fees deposited into the general fund. Do NOT quote the fiscal-note $2,000/$500 figures as enacted law.
  • Manufacturer penalty — §44-95-65(K): Manufacturer offering an ENDS product not listed on the directory for sale is subject to a $1,000-daily fine for each product until removed or properly listed.
  • Removal grace periods — §44-95-65(L): If material change requires removal, distributor has 21 days and retailer has 42 days from removal to remove from inventory and return to manufacturer for disposal.
  • Enforcement/seizure — §44-95-65(M): AG, SLED, DOR, or any state/local law enforcement agency may enforce and seize/destroy non-directory ENDS products at end of grace periods, cost borne by distributor/retailer seized from.
  • Retail ban and sell-through — §44-95-65(N): Except as provided in (N)(2)–(3), beginning 1 Feb 2027, or on the date AG first makes the directory available for public inspection on its official website, whichever is later, ENDS products not included in the directory may not be sold for retail sale in SC, directly or through importer/distributor/wholesaler/retailer/intermediary. Each retailer has 60 calendar days from directory publication to sell inventory not included or remove it; each distributor/wholesaler has 60 calendar days to remove intended-for-SC inventory. After 60 calendar days following publication, non-directory ENDS products intended for retail sale are subject to seizure, forfeiture, and destruction, and may not be purchased or sold for retail sale; no ENDS products may be seized from a consumer who made a bona fide purchase.
  • Retailer licence condition — §44-95-65(O): “A retailer shall not sell ENDS products without holding a valid South Carolina Retail License and disclosing the sale of tobacco or ENDS products on the Business Tax Application filed with the South Carolina Department of Revenue. Failure to comply… constitutes a violation subject to all fines and penalties imposed by the South Carolina Department of Revenue.”
  • Importer/retailer/wholesaler/distributor ban and civil penalties — §44-95-65(Q)–(R): No importer, retailer, wholesaler, or distributor may sell/offer/distribute an ENDS product not listed on the directory. Civil penalty: not more than $500 first violation; at least $750 but not more than $1,000 second within 36 months; at least $1,000 but not more than $1,500 third within 36 months; at least $1,500 but not more than $3,000 fourth or subsequent within 36 months. False representation by manufacturer is a misdemeanor per representation (§44-95-65(S)); any other violation is a $500 fine per offense (§44-95-65(T)); violation of (Q) is an unfair/deceptive trade practice under Title 39, Chapter 5 (§44-95-65(V)).
  • Marketing/label restrictions — §44-95-65(X)–(Y): No manufacturer/distributor/retailer may sell/offer/advertise/distribute ENDS products using, in labelling/packaging/advertising/marketing: terms “candy,” “candies,” “bubble gum,” “cotton candy,” “gummy bear,” “lollipop,” “cake,” “cupcake,” “pie,” “ice cream,” “sherbert,” “popsicle,” “bomb pop” or variants; images/references to children's toys, cartoons, cartoon characters, superheroes, television shows, video games, movies, or similar characters commonly used to market to minors; trade dress/trademarks/imagery imitating food brands/products commonly marketed to minors or school supplies. Advertising only where at least 85% of intended audience is reasonably expected to be 18+ (reliable, up-to-date audience composition data or event organizer restrictions); no materially false/untrue statements inconsistent with labelling; no health/therapeutic claims.
  • Age proof — §44-95-65(AA): Unlawful to sell an ENDS product to an individual who does not present, upon demand, proper proof of age. Failure to demand ID is not a defence. Proof demanded, shown, and reasonably relied upon is a defence.
  • Timelines — Act §2: First certification required by 1 Jan 2027; directory operational by 1 Feb 2027, or on the date AG first makes it available, whichever is later; AG shall notify retailers/wholesalers/distributors when operational; §44-95-65(K) and (Q) effective on the date the directory is operational.
  • Definition change — Act §3, §16-17-501(3) “Electronic smoking device” as amended: “any device that may be used to deliver any aerosolized or vaporized substance, including e-liquid, to the person inhaling from the device including, but not limited to, an e-cigarette, e-cigar, e-pipe, vape pen, or e-hookah. 'Electronic smoking device' includes any component, part, or accessory of the device, and also includes any substance intended to be aerosolized or vaporized during the use of the device whether or not the substance includes nicotine. 'Electronic smoking device' also includes any ENDS product, as defined by Section 44-95-65. 'Electronic smoking device' does not include drugs, devices, or combination products authorized for sale by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, as those terms are defined in the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.” Nuance: The amended “electronic smoking device” definition is broad (any aerosolized substance, whether or not nicotine), while the ENDS directory definition is nicotine-only. Whether a THC/hemp vape falls under §16-17-500 sale-to-minor rules via the broad device definition, and whether it falls in the ENDS directory, are two different questions — [VERIFY both classifications before stating either].
  • Do not merge S.287 and H.3728: A different bill, H.3728 (Jan 2025), for a similar AG directory, “as of early 2026, this bill remains pending in the House and has not become law” (LegalClarity, different article). S.287 is the enacted Act No. 97; H.3728 is not. Still to verify: The date AG first makes the directory available for public inspection (this triggers the (N) ban and sell-through clocks) — that date was not located in this session.
  • Federal ENDS context — secondary: As of FDA's most recent enforcement data in the secondary summary, only 41 e-cigarette products hold FDA marketing authorization and are the only ones that may lawfully be sold in the US; FDA has issued civil penalty complaints against nearly 200 brick-and-mortar and online retailers for unauthorised products — secondary, [VERIFY FDA list/count before use].

  • Current SC law: NO statewide minimum age for hemp-derived THC products and NO statewide minimum age for CBD products in enacted statute (Run 1 §1.5, confirmed again in this session by absence of any age provision in Chapter 55 as retrieved). Retailer 18+ or 21+ policies are voluntary/store policy, not state law. Do not state “21+ to buy CBD in SC” as law.

PROPOSED only, H.3924 failed 25 June 2026 — do not quote the 21+ possession rule as law.
    • H.3935 secondary summary: 21+ — PROPOSED only, [VERIFY official text].
    • H.4758/H.4759 and other 2025–2026 hemp bills: 21+ in secondary summaries — PROPOSED only.
  • Tobacco/vaping age does NOT automatically set a hemp age: §16-17-500 (state 18) and federal Tobacco 21 (21) apply to tobacco products and alternative nicotine products as defined in §16-17-501. A hemp/CBD product that is not a tobacco/alternative nicotine product is not covered by that age rule on the text retrieved; a hemp vape that IS marketed/sold as an alternative nicotine product or ENDS product could fall under tobacco/ENDS rules — that classification question is [VERIFY — do not resolve it without the §16-17-501 definitions and enacted ENDS definition] (see §12.1.4 nuance).
