No statewide “no minors in CBD shops” rule was located.
  • Federal age rules that do NOT create a SC hemp age: Federal Tobacco 21 (21 for tobacco/nicotine), federal alcohol 21, and any FDA rules for approved drugs (e.g. Epidiolex prescription age/prescriber rules) do not set a SC hemp/CBD retail age. Do not import them.

12.3 Impaired driving law and testing

  • Statute: SC Code §56-5-2930, unlawful to operate a motor vehicle while under the influence of alcohol, drugs, or like substances.
  • Impairment standard — statutory text as quoted in the 2025 Code text (ArkLegal) and in S.52 bill text quoting the current section (ArkLegal, §56-5-2930 (2025); S.52, 28 Jan 2026 version; S.52, 5 Feb 2026 version; all accessed 2026-10-24): §56-5-2930(A): “It is unlawful for a person to drive a motor vehicle within this State while under the influence of alcohol to the extent that the person's faculties to drive a motor vehicle are materially and appreciably impaired, under the influence of any other drug or a combination of other drugs or substances which cause impairment to the extent that the person's faculties to drive a motor vehicle are materially and appreciably impaired, or under the combined influence of alcohol and any other drug or drugs or substances which cause impairment to the extent that the person's faculties to drive a motor vehicle are materially and appreciably impaired.” Flag: This wording is confirmed in two independent reproductions of the current section, but the current scstatehouse.gov §56-5-2930 page itself was not opened in this session — [VERIFY current text on scstatehouse.gov before final quotation]. Secondary law-firm summary (John Newkirk Law) agrees: there is no separate “marijuana DUI” law; whether alcohol, marijuana, prescription medication, or combination, the charge is the same DUI. John Newkirk Law (secondary). Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • No per-se THC limit: Secondary consensus in this session (John Newkirk Law) states: for alcohol, BAC 0.08 or higher automatically creates a legal inference of impairment; no such threshold exists for THC; prosecution must prove marijuana materially and appreciably impaired ability to drive, and proving impairment from THC is far more difficult than from alcohol. No SC per-se THC blood/urine threshold (e.g. 5 ng/mL) was located in current law. A 5 ng/mL driving threshold appears ONLY in a secondary claim about a proposed H.4759-type compromise (Run 1 §1.9, flagged as not adopted, likely confusion with H.3924) — do NOT present 5 ng/mL as SC law. S.53 proposed §56-5-3910 (vaporizing while driving) is PROPOSED only.
  • DUAC is alcohol-only on the retrieved summaries: Touma Law Group states a separate law makes it illegal to drive with an unlawful alcohol content of 0.08 percent or higher, sometimes called DUAC, with the same penalties as DUI. DUAC (§56-5-2933) is an alcohol-concentration offence, not a THC offence — do not present DUAC as a THC per-se rule. Touma Law Group (secondary). Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • DUI penalties — base tier statutory, alcohol tiers secondary, do not apply alcohol tiers to a THC-only case:
    • First offense, §56-5-2930(A)(1) as quoted in the 2025 text: “by a fine of four hundred dollars or imprisonment for not less than forty-eight hours nor more than thirty days.” In lieu of the 48-hour minimum imprisonment, the court may provide for 48 hours of public service employment, served at a time when the person is not working and does not interfere with regular employment; the court may not compel public service employment in lieu of the minimum 48-hour sentence.
    • Alcohol-concentration tiers in the same section (secondary summary, Touma): if alcohol concentration is at least 0.10% but less than 0.16%, fine $500 or 72 hours to 30 days; at 0.16% or higher, fine $1,000 or 30 to 90 days (Touma summary phrases the first tier as “under a 0.10 percent BAC” with near-$992 with assessments/surcharges, and every tier carrying a six-month licence suspension; second offense $2,100–$5,100 and 5 days to 1 year, one-year suspension; third offense $3,800–$6,300 and 60 days to 3 years, two-year suspension, four years if within five years of first, vehicle confiscation if within ten years of first — all secondary, [VERIFY current §56-5-2930 penalty tiers, licence suspensions, and ten-year lookback before quoting beyond the first-offense base tier]).
    • General DUI penalty structure beyond the first-offense base tier, licence suspension, ignition interlock, felony DUI, and child endangerment were NOT verified in this session from the current §§56-5-2930/56-5-2941/56-5-2945/56-5-2947 texts. Do NOT import an alcohol-DUI penalty table into Part 12 without opening those sections.
  • Implied consent — §56-5-2950 (secondary/2025 summary and old amendment text, [VERIFY current text, time limits, and personnel/site rules]):
    • A person who drives a motor vehicle in SC is considered to have given consent to chemical tests of breath, blood, or urine for purpose of determining presence of alcohol, drugs, or combination, if arrested for offence arising out of acts alleged to have been committed while driving while under influence of alcohol, drugs, or combination (arklegal.ai, citing §56-5-2950 (2025)). ArkLegal, §56-5-2950 (2025). Accessed 2026-10-24.
    • Breath test must be administered at direction of arresting officer; person first must be offered breath test to determine alcohol concentration; if physically unable to provide acceptable breath sample because injured mouth, unconscious, dead, or other reason acceptable to licensed medical personnel, arresting officer may request blood sample.
    • If officer has reasonable suspicion (old text: reasonable grounds) to believe person is under influence of drugs other than alcohol, or combination of alcohol and drugs, officer may order urine sample for testing.
    • Breath sample taken for testing must be collected within two hours of arrest; any additional tests to collect other samples must be collected within three hours of arrest (2025 summary — [VERIFY time limits in current text]).
    • Breath test must be administered by person trained/certified by SC Criminal Justice Academy, pursuant to SLED policies (2025 summary; old text says SLED-trained/certified, methods approved by SLED); arresting officer may not administer tests; blood/urine tests must be administered by physicians licensed by State Board of Medical Examiners, registered nurses licensed by State Board of Nursing, and other medical personnel trained to administer such tests in licensed medical facility (old text — [VERIFY current personnel/site rules, as S.52-type amendments propose expanding to laboratory technicians, phlebotomists, EMTs]).
    • Do NOT quote the old 0.10% figure: Old text also states if breathalyzer reading is 0.10% by weight or above, officer may not require additional tests — that 0.10% figure is historical (pre-0.08) and must NOT be quoted as current law without checking current §56-5-2950 inference provisions. An old amendment snippet (1987–1988 Bill 25, scstatehouse.gov) adding “'drug' means illicit or licit drug, a combination of licit or illicit drugs, a combination of alcohol and an illicit drug or a combination of alcohol and a licit drug” to §56-5-2930 is likewise historical, not a substitute for current text.
  • Testing methods for marijuana impairment — secondary only:
    • No breathalyzer for marijuana (secondary consensus).
    • Field sobriety tests: walk-and-turn, one-leg stand, horizontal gaze nystagmus (HGN) — originally designed to detect alcohol impairment, reliability for marijuana impairment widely questioned by defence attorneys/toxicology experts (secondary, John Newkirk Law).
    • Drug Recognition Expert (DRE) evaluation: SC officers trained as DREs may conduct 12-step evaluation protocol looking for pupil dilation, muscle tone, vital signs, behavioural indicators; DRE evaluations carry weight in court but are inherently subjective and vulnerable to challenge (secondary, same source).
    • Blood/urine toxicology can show presence of THC/metabolites, but presence alone does not prove the “materially and appreciably impaired” standard under the secondary summary — that inference must be labelled secondary, not a statutory rule, and the distinction between presence and impairment is the key Part 12 point.
  • Pending DUI bill — PROPOSED only, status NOT checked: S.52, 126th General Assembly (Davis, Cash, Gambrell, Grooms, Jackson, Devine, Climer, Johnson, Adams, Turner, Kimbrell, Sutton, Blackmon, Williams, Alexander, Verdin, Garrett, Zell, Walker; similar H.4005), summary in search (scstatehouse.gov billsearch, 3 May 2026 timestamp): would amend §56-5-2930 penalty provisions to permit sentences of both fines and incarceration and require DUI Victim Impact Panels; amend §56-5-2933 similarly; amend §56-5-2941 (ignition interlock) to delete provision that nothing requires installation prior to contested hearings; amend §56-5-2945 to create felony DUI second degree, penalties, define “moderate bodily injury”; amend §56-5-2947 (child endangerment) to include reckless vehicular homicide and reckless driving; amend §56-5-2950 to revise circumstances/procedures/test sites, provide laboratory technicians/phlebotomists/EMTs may obtain blood/urine samples, revise suspension periods for refusal and certain alcohol concentrations, revise provision that §§56-1-1320 and 56-5-2990 (alcohol/drug safety action program, provisional licence) will not be effective until ignition interlock restricted licence period completed. S.52 status (enacted/pending/dead) was NOT checked — [VERIFY S.52 official history before mentioning it at all, and present it as PROPOSED if mentioned].
  • No SC cannabis-specific driving rule for Julian's Law patients was located: Julian's Law immunity in §44-53-1840 covers use/prescription/administration/possession/manufacture/distribution in compliance with Article 18, but does NOT on its face authorise driving while impaired, and S.53's proposed vaporizing-while-driving provision (§56-5-3910) is PROPOSED only. Do not present Julian's Law as a driving defence.

12.4 Expungement and record clearing for marijuana offences

Headline — secondary consensus: South Carolina has NO marijuana-specific expungement process and NO automatic expungement for marijuana convictions (Marijuana Herald, “Marijuana Expungement Laws by State: Can You Clear a Marijuana Conviction in 2026?”, updated 39 days before search — “South Carolina | General relief | South Carolina has no marijuana-specific process. General conviction relief is relatively narrow and applies primarily to certain misdemeanor offenses.”; Coastal Law, “What Charges Can Be Expunged in SC?”, updated 22 days before search — “In all cases except 30-day misdemeanors, you must initiate the expungement process and it is not automatic.”). Both are secondary; the “no automatic” point must be presented as secondary-supported, with the statutory routes below as the official framework.

Otherwise, three years from the date of conviction.” The “immediately” point is secondary phrasing for the (B) application route, not a statutory “automatic” rule — label as secondary. Other Coastal Law secondary waiting periods: most 30-day misdemeanors three years from conviction; CDV third degree five years; fraudulent check one year; failure to stop for blue light three years after completion if no bodily injury; Youthful Offender Act conviction five years after completion if no other convictions during that time.
  • What is NOT expungeable / limits — secondary only: Traffic cases including DUI and DUAC generally cannot be expunged (Coastal Law secondary); exceptions: reckless driving charges can now be sent to PTI and expunged, meaning in prosecutor's discretion a DUI charge can be sent to PTI if ticket re-written as reckless driving; failure to stop for blue light can be expunged three years after completion if no bodily injury; minor traffic offences can be expunged on completion of Traffic Education Program (TEP), technically dismissal/expungement with no conviction. Second/subsequent marijuana possession, distribution/manufacture, and trafficking offences do NOT fit the first-offence routes above on the retrieved summaries; no broad “all marijuana convictions” expungement law was located. Do not present second/subsequent offences as expungeable under §44-53-450 (once only, first offence, no prior) or §22-5-910 (first offence, 30-day misdemeanor) without a specific statutory basis.
  • Pardon is a separate executive route (Governor / Board of Paroles and Pardons) and was NOT researched in this session — do not present pardon as an expungement route, and flag as a gap if pardon is to be included.
  • Proposed expansion — PROPOSED only, status not checked: H.3730, 2025–2026, “Expungement,” scstatehouse.gov H.3730 bill page (via search, 41 days before search; accessed 2026-10-24): TO AMEND SC Code BY ADDING §17-22-915 SO AS TO ALLOW EXPUNGEMENT OF FIRST OFFENSE NONVIOLENT OFFENSES AND DRUG TREATMENT COURT OFFENSES AFTER CERTAIN TIME PERIODS WITHOUT PENDING CHARGES OR ADDITIONAL CONVICTIONS; BY AMENDING §17-22-910 (applications) to reference §17-22-915; BY AMENDING §17-22-940 (expungement process) to provide verification of eligibility by court for drug treatment court participants before expungement. Proposed §17-22-915(A): person convicted on first offence for nonviolent offence, as defined in §16-1-70, may apply to appropriate solicitor's office for expungement provided no pending charges and no conviction of any other offence for ten years from date of conviction. (B) Person who successfully completes drug treatment court programme for first-offence conviction for nonviolent offence may apply provided no pending charges and no conviction of any other offence for three years from date of completion of drug treatment court programme. (C) No person may have records expunged under section more than once. After expungement, SLED required to keep nonpublic record of offence and date of expungement. H.3730 official history/enactment was NOT checked — present as PROPOSED only, do not present §17-22-915 as current law.

The search term “South Carolina Second Chance Act” returned general expungement summaries and H.3730, not a named Second Chance Act. Do not import DC's Second Chance Act (from other-state memory) into SC. Follow-up if wanted: search scstatehouse.gov for “Second Chance” as a short title, not as an assumed SC law.

12.5 Landlord and tenant rules

  • No cannabis-specific landlord/tenant statute was located in this session. No SC statute creating a tenant protection for lawful hemp/CBD use, a medical cannabis housing protection, or a landlord right to evict solely for hemp/CBD use was located [UNAVAILABLE/VERIFY — Title 27, Chapter 40 was not opened in full].
  • General framework: SC Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, SC Code Title 27, Chapter 40, §§27-40-10 et seq. (secondary LegalClarity summary, LegalClarity (secondary), updated 586 days before search, accessed 2026-10-24).
  • Secondary eviction grounds — label as secondary and [VERIFY §§27-40-710 and 27-40-740 in current Code]:
    • Nonpayment of rent: §27-40-710, landlord can initiate eviction if tenant fails to pay rent on agreed date; grace period not required unless explicitly stated in lease (secondary).
    • Lease violations: §27-40-710(B), if tenant breaches lease — e.g. unauthorised pets, exceeding occupancy limits, damaging property — landlord can seek removal; tenant must be given opportunity to correct within legally required timeframe; if fails, proceedings continue (secondary).
    • Illegal activity on premises: §27-40-740 does NOT create an illegal-activity eviction right — §27-40-740 is “Landlord's lien; distress proceeding.” Illegal/drug-related conduct, if it is a lease/§27-40-510 breach, falls under §27-40-710(A) (written notice, termination date not less than 14 days after receipt, cure within 14 days or good-faith commencement) or §27-40-720 (health/safety). No immediate, no-notice illegal-activity termination provision was found in §§27-40-710/-720/-740 as opened [AUDITED — original secondary claim deleted]; law enforcement involvement strengthens landlord's case, though conviction is not necessarily required (secondary, LegalClarity). A second secondary summary (StateRegsToday) states landlords must follow proper legal procedures and provide notice before evicting for criminal activity, and tenants may have defences (not involved, landlord had knowledge and failed to act) — secondary conflict on notice for illegal-activity evictions, carry both and flag [VERIFY §27-40-740 notice/cure text].
    • General tenant-protection summary (StateRegsToday, secondary): under SC Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, landlords have right to terminate/evict for violation of any law/ordinance imposing code restrictions on use/maintenance of property, including criminal activity such as drug-related offences or violent crimes, but must follow proper procedures and provide notice — again, secondary, [VERIFY].
  • Lease form language — NOT statute (secondary forms, do not present as law):

    • Generic SC month-to-month / standard lease forms (secondary, ailawyer.com / dottedsign.com): tenant in default if tenant/guests/occupants violate agreement or fire/safety/health/criminal laws regardless of arrest/conviction; or are arrested/convicted/given deferred adjudication for criminal offence involving actual/potential physical harm, or involving possession/manufacture/delivery of controlled substance, marijuana, or drug paraphernalia under SC statute; or illegal drugs/paraphernalia found in premises or on person of tenant/guests/occupants while on premises; on default landlord may seek all remedies including eviction, tenant liable for costs including reasonable attorneys' fees. These are form clauses, enforceability depends on the signed lease and the Act — do not present form language as a statutory eviction ground.

12.6 Gun ownership conflicts

  • Federal baseline for this section — label as federal law, not SC law:
    • 18 USC §922(g)(3): unlawful user of or addicted to a controlled substance is prohibited from possessing firearms/ammunition. Secondary CWP-eligibility summary (LegalClarity, LegalClarity (secondary), updated 80 days before search, accessed 2026-10-24) lists federal disqualifiers under §922(g) including: convicted of crime punishable by more than one year in prison; fugitive from justice; unlawful user of or addicted to controlled substance; involuntarily committed/adjudicated mentally defective; unlawfully in country or most nonimmigrant visas; dishonourably discharged; renounced US citizenship; subject to qualifying domestic violence protective order; convicted of misdemeanor crime of domestic violence. Each category comes from federal statute and applies regardless of SC law (secondary summary of federal statute — [VERIFY 18 USC §922(g) text before quoting the list as law]).
    • ATF Form 4473 unlawful-user question and “unlawful user” definition are federal, not SC, and were not opened in this session — flag [VERIFY ATF Form 4473 / 27 CFR §478.11 current text].
    • Fourth Circuit case law — secondary (Axelrod & Associates, Axelrod (secondary), updated 1335 days before search, i.e. ~2022, pre-dating the 2026 federal developments below): Wilson v. Lynch, 2016, 9th Cir., held it did not violate Second Amendment rights to prevent purchase solely because person held medical marijuana card, even though government offered no evidence of use and person denied use; United States v. Carter, 2012, 4th Cir. (which includes SC), found marijuana users can be prohibited under §922(g), calling marijuana users “dangerous and non-law abiding citizens” categorically excluded from historical scope of Anglo-American right to bear arms, comparing pot smokers to domestic violence abusers (secondary paraphrase, not a quotation — do not quote that language as a court holding without opening Carter). The Axelrod article's headline premise — “medical marijuana cardholders are prohibited from owning a firearm” — is about other states' cardholders, because SC HAS NO medical marijuana card. In SC, the relevant federal question is unlawful use, not cardholding, and there is no SC card to trigger a Wilson-type card-based denial. That distinction must be stated explicitly.
    • Post-2026 federal development — from federal Run 2 memory in standing context, NOT re-verified in this SC session and NOT in the SC task's federal baseline — carry as [VERIFY — do not present as settled SC law without a fresh federal check]: US v. Hemani, No. 24-1234, decided 18 June 2026, Gorsuch, held a status-only 18 USC §922(g)(3) prosecution of a regular marijuana user for in-home possession, with no danger showing, inconsistent with the Second Amendment (as-applied, narrow); ATF interim final rule eff. 22 Jan 2026 rewrote 27 CFR 478.11 to require regular use continuing into the present; Schedule III alone does not remove medical users from §922(g)(3) text and no ATF safe harbour was located [VERIFY in federal Run 2]. If Hemani is included in SC Part 12, it must be presented as a narrow federal as-applied holding, not as a SC licence, not as a general right for SC marijuana users to possess firearms, and not as a defence to a SC state firearms charge.
    • No ATF safe harbour for SC Julian's Law CBD users, SC hemp users, or SC medical users was located in this session [UNAVAILABLE]. Do not present hemp/CBD use as automatically outside §922(g)(3) — hemp is not a Schedule I/II controlled substance federally, but the federal “unlawful user” question turns on controlled-substance use, and a product that is marijuana under federal/SC law (e.g. >0.3% delta-9, or isomer product treated as marijuana) is not hemp. That application is analytical, not a located ATF ruling.
  • SC state firearms law — secondary summaries, [VERIFY current Code sections before quoting]:
    • SC is a “shall issue” state for Concealed Weapons Permits (CWP) issued by SLED (secondary, US Legal Forms / LegalClarity). Constitutional carry / permitless carry, secondary (Ferrari Firearms guide, updated 168 days before search, Ferrari Firearms (secondary), accessed 2026-10-24): effective 7 Mar 2024, Governor Henry McMaster signed SC Constitutional Carry / Second Amendment Preservation Act; any person legally permitted to possess firearm under state and federal law may carry concealed handgun without permit; must be at least 18; must not be prohibited under state/federal law; all other location restrictions still apply; duty to inform law enforcement if asked; CWP remains available, minimum age 21 for CWP, 8-hour approved course, application to SLED, fee $50 new / the rejected lower renewal figure (secondary, conflicts with scstatehouse.gov query snippet in search stating CWP renewal fee $50, waived for disabled veterans/retired law enforcement, and permit valid for four years in that snippet vs five years in Ferrari guide — carry fee/validity conflict, [VERIFY current §23-31-210 et seq.]); open carry of long guns allowed without permit, open carry of handgun allowed with CWP or under constitutional carry (secondary).

US LawShield SC gun laws summary (US LawShield (secondary), via search, accessed 2026-10-24) agrees in substance and cites §§23-31-410, 415, 420 for testing.
    • Carrying into alcohol business — secondary, [VERIFY section numbers and penalties]: Person otherwise lawfully carrying a firearm prohibited from knowingly carrying into business selling alcohol for consumption if prohibited by “NO CONCEALABLE WEAPONS ALLOWED” sign in compliance with §23-31-325, or requested to leave/remove weapon, or consuming alcoholic liquor/beer/wine; on conviction fine not more than $2,000 or imprisonment not more than two years, or both (secondary, citing §16-23-465 in one line — the search snippet mixes §§23-31-325, 23-31-400–420, and 16-23-465; verify).
    • SC unlawful possession by violent-crime felons — secondary (US Legal Forms, via search): §16-23-30(A) — unlawful for person convicted of violent crime, as defined by §16-1-60, classified as felony, to possess firearm/ammunition within SC; misdemeanor “crime of violence” list includes murder, manslaughter (except negligent manslaughter arising from traffic accidents), rape, mayhem, kidnapping, burglary, robbery, housebreaking, assault with intent to kill/commit rape/rob, assault with dangerous weapon, etc. (secondary list, [VERIFY §§16-23-30 and 16-1-60]). A simple marijuana possession misdemeanor (≤1 oz, ≤30 days) is NOT a violent-crime felony on that list, so it does not by itself trigger the SC violent-felony firearm ban on the retrieved summaries — but a felony distribution/trafficking conviction, or a felony drug conviction punishable by more than one year, can trigger federal §922(g)(1) (crime punishable by more than one year) and, if violent, SC §16-23-30. That application must be labelled analytical, not a located SC ruling on marijuana felonies.

Relevant to SC trafficking cases with firearms, but NOT a SC statute — label as federal.

    • Practical conflict summary for Part 12: (1) SC has no medical card, so there is no SC card-based federal denial to discuss; (2) unlawful marijuana use in SC can still trigger federal §922(g)(3) on the pre-Hemani Carter/Wilson framework, subject to Hemani's narrow as-applied limit [VERIFY]; (3) SC constitutional carry / CWP does NOT override federal prohibition — a person must be legally permitted under BOTH state and federal law to carry under the secondary constitutional-carry summary; (4) using/discharging a firearm while under influence of a controlled substance is separately prohibited/tested under SC §§23-31-400–420 (secondary/2021 Code text, Verify); (5) a felony marijuana conviction can trigger federal and, if violent, state firearm bans, while a first simple possession misdemeanor does not on its face trigger the SC violent-felony ban.

12.7 Pet and veterinary products

  • SC Board of Veterinary Medical Examiners FAQ — OPENED in this session: LLR Board of Veterinary Medical Examiners FAQ (SC Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation, Synergy Business Park, Kingstree Building, 110 Centerview Dr., Columbia, SC 29210, (803) 896-4300, office hours 8:30am–5:00pm, Office of Inspector General 1-855-723-7283 — public agency contact, not personal). Accessed 2026-10-24.
    • Q10, “Can licensed veterinarians treat and/or prescribe animals supplements containing cannabis derivatives?” — opened text: “Currently, there are no approved animal drugs derived from cannabis. Animal drugs must generally receive premarket approval by FDA via the New Animal Drug Application (NADA) process. The manufacture and marketing/sales of drugs in interstate that have not been FDA approved is a violation of federal law. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulates drugs, food, and medical devices for humans and animals. Such products require FDA approval in order to be legal. The FDA regulates dietary supplements through Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act (DSHEA). And states: 'Dietary supplements are products for humans and does not include products for animals. 21 U.S.C. §321(ff)(1)(E).'” Link in FAQ to SCDA notice: SCDA CBD/hemp food-and-feed notice (linked, NOT opened as a page in this session — follow-up: open it).
    • Q11, “Is it legal for veterinarians to sell CBD products?” — opened text: “It largely depends on the intended use of the product and how it is labeled and marketed. Even if a CBD product meets the definition of 'hemp' under the 2018 Farm Bill, its marketing and sale must comply with other applicable laws, including the FDA and its regulations and those at the state level. FDA has expressed its concern regarding products containing CBD and other cannabis-derived compounds that are being marketed for therapeutic use without approval by FDA. They have stated that, 'Selling unapproved products with unsubstantiated therapeutic claims is not only a violation of the law, but can also put patients at risk, as the products have not been proven to be safe or effective.'” Therapeutic claims include not only label but also promotion (websites, advertisements, circulars, testimonials) suggesting intended use(s). Marketing unapproved treatments raises possibility owners may use them in lieu of approved therapies, leading to treatment failures/increased suffering. Use of unapproved drugs can put patients at risk and may create legal risk for veterinarians who administer, prescribe, dispense, or recommend them because they have not been evaluated for efficacy/safety by FDA; risk heightened when approved treatments available and not utilised, or when patients adversely impacted (side effects or treatment failures).
    • Q12, “My state has laws that allow cannabis to be sold for medical use without FDA approval. Doesn't that mean, as a veterinarian, that I can legally use and/or recommend them for my patients?” — opened text: “No. To date, laws that have been passed by states that remove state restrictions on the use of cannabis for medical or recreational use by people do not apply to their use in animals.” That answer applies a fortiori in SC, which has no general medical/recreational law at all — but do not present Q12 as a SC-specific rule; it is a Board FAQ restating the federal/state distinction.
    • Q9, therapeutic options/alternate therapies: SC Code §40-69-20(17) defines therapeutic options/alternate therapies as including acupuncture, manipulation/adjustment, magnetic field therapy, holistic medicine, homeopathy, herbology/naturopathy, massage, physical therapy; §40-69-270(C) allows veterinarians to delegate therapeutic options/alternate therapies to person whose qualifications/competencies veterinarian has verified prior to delegation; delegating veterinarian remains responsible for general care of patient. This is NOT a cannabis authorisation — do not present herbology/naturopathy in §40-69-20(17) as a CBD prescription authority.
    • Q13, compounding: 26 June 2020, SC Board of Pharmacy Regulations amended to address compounding of veterinary drug preparations, Reg. 99–47: licensed pharmacist in permitted pharmacy may compound veterinary drug preparations for veterinarians' office administration; compounded office-use preparations may be dispensed by veterinarian to owner for treatment of bodily injury/disease only in urgent/emergency situation for single course of treatment, not to exceed 168-hour supply; may not be distributed by entity other than compounding pharmacy, except administration in veterinary healthcare setting or dispensing pursuant to prescription drug order under federal/state law. Again, NOT a CBD authorisation.

12.8 CBD/low-THC use in schools

  • Current school tobacco/alternative nicotine policy — SC Code §59-1-380, via Justia 2025 and 2021 texts in search (Justia, §59-1-380; Justia 2021, §59-1-380; accessed 2026-10-24):
    • 2025 Justia text, (A): “Every local school district in the State shall implement and enforce a written policy prohibiting at all times the use of any tobacco product by any person in school buildings, in school facilities, on school campuses, and in or on any other school property owned or operated by the local school administrative unit. The policy also must prohibit the use of any tobacco product by persons attending a school-sponsored event at a location not listed in this subsection when in the presence of students or school personnel or in an area where smoking or other tobacco use is otherwise prohibited by law.”
    • 2021 Justia text, (A): “By August 1, 2019, every local school district in the State shall adopt, implement, and enforce a written policy prohibiting at all times the use of any tobacco product or alternative nicotine product by any person in school buildings, in school facilities, on school campuses, and in or on any other school property owned or operated by the local school administrative unit. The policy also must prohibit the use of any tobacco product or alternative nicotine product by persons attending a school-sponsored event at a location not listed in this subsection when in the presence of students or school personnel or in an area where smoking or other tobacco use is otherwise prohibited by law.”
    • (B) Policy must include: (1) adequate notice to students, parents/guardians, public, school personnel; (2) posting of signs prohibiting at all times use of tobacco/alternative nicotine products by any person in/on school property; (3) requirements school personnel enforce policy, including appropriate disciplinary action.
